extraction.framework: ClawVM
extraction.topology: single-agent OpenClaw-style harness with a virtual-memory layer interposed at prompt assembly, tool mediation and lifecycle hooks
extraction.benchmark: Custom: four synthetic OpenClaw-derived workload families across six token budgets (120-500), six Tier-1 lifecycle regression scenarios, 12 trace-derived replays of real Claude Code sessions, 30 task-level replays, three adversarial scenarios and 20 live single-session tasks
extraction.baseline: Retrieval (no caching or writeback), Retrieval+Cache, Compaction-Hybrid (a practitioner-configured prefetch plus compaction-writeback policy), an offline Oracle with a 3-turn horizon, and an LRU variant retaining the same structural features
extraction.key_results: Mean explicit policy-controllable faults per workload-budget configuration fall from 67.8 (Retrieval), 10.8 (Retrieval+Cache) and 1.5 (Compaction-Hybrid) to zero, with thrash reduced by 77.4%, 45.2% and 11.4% respectively, and the offline oracle confirms no remaining headroom on fault count. At the tightest 120-token budget Compaction-Hybrid incurs 26 faults across four workloads including 7 bootstrap and 5 flush-miss. On 30 task-level replays ClawVM reaches 100% success at budgets 180 and 300 while Compaction-Hybrid drops to 76.7% at budget 180, with all 7 failures being bootstrap faults in debugging tasks. Across 12 real session traces ClawVM records zero faults versus a Retrieval median of 51 (range 49-77), rising to a median of 83 at 200 turns. Policy-engine overhead is a median of 18-44 microseconds per turn with p95 under 60 microseconds and under 83 KB peak memory. Ablation: pointer resolution alone removes 84% of faults (271 to 43), and an LRU upgrade heuristic with the same structural features also reaches zero faults.
extraction.limitations: Semantic correctness is explicitly out of scope: the system validates schema, provenance, scope and non-destructiveness but does not verify the truth of model-generated updates. The replay engine models tool calls by canonical signature without executing real tools, so non-deterministic services are not covered. The live experiment exercises only 20 single-session tasks, leaving cross-session lifecycle edges replay-validated only, and claims are scoped to structural lifecycle faults rather than semantic correctness or end-to-end task quality, since deterministic replay isolates policy behaviour but not online effects such as model non-determinism and tool latency.
extraction.varied_factor: memory (harness-level residency, compaction and writeback policy)

records.title: Co-Harness: Co-Evolving Harnesses and Model Weights for LLM Agents

evidence_notes.summary: Co-Harness is the clearest statement in the set that the harness is not merely a confounder but part of the data-generating process, since the trajectories used for post-training are themselves produced by the harness. For RQ1 the most useful number is the +24.7 pp average margin of the co-evolved system over a carefully hand-crafted static harness on the same benchmarks and model scales, which puts an upper bound on how much a fixed human harness leaves on the table. Its failure taxonomy is directly reusable for attribution work, mapping each failure to prompt ambiguity, tool schema error, missing skill, middleware mismatch, memory overflow, or an explicit non-harness 'agent error' abstention, and it reports human inter-annotator agreement of 0.77 on that taxonomy. The paper deliberately varies both model and harness, so it cannot isolate either, and its own Harness Debt discussion concedes the risk that trajectories collected under a compensating scaffold produce models that over-rely on it. The appendix reproduces an attribution prompt template addressed to a critic model; that text is a research artifact quoted from the paper and I treated it as data, not as instructions.

quotes.text:
Existing pipelines typically train models under a fixed harness,
including prompts, tools, skills, middleware, and memory, while leaving the data-generating process
outside the optimization objective.

Crucially, R2 also surpasses the Human-designed static Harness by an average of +24.7
pp—demonstrating that the automated co-evolution not only improves over its own starting point but also
exceeds the ceiling of a carefully hand-crafted, fixed configuration.

Co-Harness requires a capable critic LLM, a minimum volume of failure trajectories for
cold-start, and significant compute for multi-round SFT.

extraction.framework: Co-Harness, with an LLM-based HarnessCritic
extraction.topology: single-agent tool-integrated reasoning loop over a multi-turn Python code interpreter, with an LLM critic operating offline over failed trajectories
extraction.benchmark: AIME 2024, AIME 2025 and HMMT February 2025, 30 problems each, scored as pass@1 averaged over multiple rollouts
extraction.baseline: Round 0, a HarnessCritic-evolved harness with no supervised fine-tuning; and Human, a human-designed static harness with no model alignment
extraction.key_results: Two rounds of co-evolution raise average accuracy from 58.5% at Round 0 to 73.5% at Round 1 and 78.9% at Round 2, a cumulative +20.4 pp across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B, with the largest single gain of +27.2 pp on HMMT25 for Qwen3-32B and the smallest of +10.6 pp on AIME24 for Qwen3-32B. Round 2 exceeds the human-designed static harness by +24.7 pp on average, 54.2% to 78.9%. A 200+ hour autonomous run produced 22 harness versions, recovering from an initial 32-second crash to 59.6%, achieving an 8.7x wall-clock speedup from 3.78 h to 1.11 h, and reaching a best ensemble of 63.3% at 2.29 h, while correctly rolling back a domain-specific prompt regression that cost about 16.5 pp. Two expert annotators labelling 200 failure trajectories reached Cohen's kappa = 0.77. The initial harness configuration is fully specified, including retry on ToolCallException with max 3 and linear backoff, sliding-window compression to the last 4k tokens, and max turns raised from 15 to 30.
extraction.limitations: Co-Harness requires a capable critic LLM, a minimum volume of failure trajectories for cold start, and significant compute for multi-round supervised fine-tuning. Attribution accuracy degrades for failure modes that require counterfactual control-flow reasoning, and structural harness redesign remains a human responsibility. The authors additionally document three empirical conditions under which the loop stops compounding: SFT plateau, harness over-patching that overwhelms weaker models, and attribution cascade where one diff repairs a deficiency while introducing another.
extraction.varied_factor: scaffold and model, deliberately co-varied (harness diffs across prompt, tools, skills and middleware, alternating with supervised fine-tuning of model weights)

records.title: From Question Answering to Task Completion: A Survey on Agent System and Harness Design

evidence_notes.summary: This survey supplies the largest body of quantitative model-versus-harness evidence in the assignment set, and it is the closest thing available to a direct answer to RQ1's magnitude question. Its central result is that conditioning on the model still leaves a median within-model range of 13.6 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.0, with 14 of 20 models varying by at least 10 points and the largest spreads exceeding 20 points, which places harness-attributable variance on the same order as a full model-generation upgrade within a fixed harness. It also shows the effect is regime-dependent: the SWE-bench Verified spread narrows to a few points for the strongest backbones while the WebArena model-only to harnessed span reaches 41.5 points for GPT-4o. Two secondary findings matter for the review. First, scaffold complexity does not predict effectiveness, since a roughly 100-line minimal scaffold nearly matches a full-featured sandbox under Opus 4.5. Second, higher accuracy is often bought with much heavier context and different timeout profiles, so harness effects are not free. The authors are explicit that this is a synthesis of uncontrolled public evidence rather than a factorial experiment, which is itself a finding for RQ2.

extraction.topology: n/a
extraction.benchmark: SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0 and WebArena as the three analysed regimes, plus a catalogue including AgentBench, OSWorld, GAIA, MLE-Bench, LoCoMo, OS-Harm, MCP-Atlas and TheAgentCompany
extraction.baseline: Model-only baselines on WebArena, and within-model or within-harness contrasts assembled from public leaderboards and source reports
extraction.key_results: Terminal-Bench 2.0, conditioning on the model: GPT-5.3-Codex spans 64.7% (Terminus 2) to 78.4% (SageAgent), a 13.7 point range; Claude Opus 4.6 spans 58.0% (Claude Code) to 76.4% (Meta-Harness), 18.4 points; Gemini 3.1 Pro spans 59.4% (Gemini CLI) to 80.2% (TongAgents), 20.8 points. Across the 20 models with at least three observed harness results the median within-model range is 13.6% and 14 of 20 vary by at least 10%. SWE-bench Verified: GPT-4o spans 23.2% (SWE-agent) to 38.8% (Agentless); Claude 3.5 Sonnet spans 33.6% (SWE-agent) to 53.6% (PatchPilot); under Opus 4.5 the roughly 100-line mini-SWE-agent reaches 76.8% against 77.6% for OpenHands + CodeAct 2.1, and vendor scaffolds lead open-source ones by 2-4 points on same-generation Claude and Gemini models. WebArena: GPT-4o spans 13.1% model-only to 54.6% with WebOperator, a 41.5 point span, and Llama-3.1-8B moves from 5.6% to 48.5%. In the opposite direction, within a fixed harness SWE-agent + tools rises from 49.0% (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) to 73.2% (Opus 4). Terminal-Bench resource statistics show accuracy differences accompanied by distinct profiles, for example Meta-Harness using a 755.0K median input context versus 79.4K for Terminus 2 on Claude Opus 4.6 while cutting the timeout rate from 18.2% to 7.9%.
extraction.limitations: The authors state that the SWE-bench Verified table is a compact synthesis of public evidence rather than a fully controlled factorial experiment, because model snapshots, reasoning settings, retry budgets and proprietary scaffold details are not aligned across sources, so only within-row-family comparisons are strong and vendor rows are upper-envelope references. The Terminal-Bench analysis is described as observational rather than a randomized ablation, since public submissions may differ in prompts, versions, budgets and implementation details. Token fields cover only 45.0% of trial records and dollar-cost fields 15.2%, so monetary cost is not used for cross-harness claims. WebArena reports mostly describe complete agent systems rather than controlled ablations. No dedicated limitations section is provided.
extraction.varied_factor: model and scaffold, through observational within-model and within-harness contrasts drawn from public leaderboards

records.title: Harness-Bench: Measuring harness effects across models in realistic agent workflows

evidence_notes.summary: Harness-Bench is the only paper in the set that makes the harness the primary axis of a full factorial design, crossing 6 harnesses with 8 model backends over 106 fixed tasks, and it is therefore the best available estimate of configuration-level harness variance under matched external conditions. The 23.8-point gap between the best and worst configurable harness under the same task set and model pool is a direct RQ1 quantity. Its most interesting secondary result is an interaction rather than a main effect: stronger backbones show lower cross-harness variance, so the share of performance attributable to the harness is itself a function of model strength, which complicates any single answer to 'how much'. The paper also localises where harness effects appear, with cross-harness variance highest in tasks requiring structured data manipulation, tool sequencing and workspace edits, and near zero in language-centric office tasks. For RQ2 its literature framing is precise: existing benchmarks either abstract away execution, conflate the harness with the whole agent, or fix the harness when comparing models, and it deliberately inverts that. Its self-imposed caveat is important, since it compares complete configurations and disclaims causal decomposition of individual mechanisms.

quotes.text:
However,
the harness itself remains largely unmeasured: existing benchmarks either abstract away execution,
conflate the harness with the full agent system, or fix the harness when comparing models.

Among
configurable harnesses, NanoBot obtains the highest aggregate score (76.2), while OpenClaw obtains
the lowest score (52.4), giving a 23.8-point gap under the same task set and model-backend pool.

Within these limits, the experiments support the central motivation of Harness-Bench:
agent capability is not fully characterized by the base model alone, but also by the execution layer
that mediates observation, action, recovery, and artifact production.

extraction.framework: Harness-Bench (evaluating OpenClaw, ZeroClaw, Hermes, Moltis, NullClaw and NanoBot, with Codex as a model-bound reference)
extraction.topology: single-agent execution harnesses, each run with its native control loop, prompting, tool interface, state policy and recovery behaviour
extraction.benchmark: Harness-Bench, 106 sandboxed offline tasks across eight workflow categories
extraction.baseline: Cross-harness comparison under a fixed task suite, budget, timeout and evaluator; Codex is reported separately as a model-bound coding-agent reference point rather than a controlled ablation
extraction.key_results: 5,194 execution trajectories from a full factorial of 106 tasks by 6 configurable harnesses by 8 API model backends (5,088) plus 106 Codex runs. Aggregate scores range from NanoBot 76.2 to OpenClaw 52.4, a 23.8-point gap under the same task set and model-backend pool, with Codex at 80.4. Stronger model backends show higher mean scores and lower cross-harness variance, implying weaker backends are more sensitive to the surrounding execution substrate. Recurring failure symptoms among failed trajectories are contract or format violations 36.4%, tool or recovery failures 24.6%, evidence or grounding gaps 14.6%, artifact commitment 11.1% and state or continuation 9.3%. Category-level cross-harness variance is highest for Data, BI and Finance Analytics at 0.0155 and lowest for Office and Business Communication at 0.0020. Token usage varies from 68.7K (NanoBot) to 175.1K (NullClaw) despite NanoBot scoring highest among configurable harnesses.
extraction.limitations: The benchmark covers controlled sandboxed offline workflows, improving reproducibility at the cost of live services, user feedback, changing external state and long-term production memory. It evaluates complete harness configurations rather than isolated mechanisms, so results are configuration-level diagnostics of model-harness pairings and not causal decompositions of individual harness mechanisms. Some process-level scores rely on rubric-based or LLM-assisted assessment using claude-sonnet-4.6 as a fixed external judge, and the results are descriptive measurements over a fixed task suite rather than statistical claims about all agent workflows.
extraction.varied_factor: scaffold (complete harness configuration) and model backend, in a full factorial

records.title: Inside the scaffold: A source-code taxonomy of coding agent architectures

evidence_notes.summary: This paper names the RQ1 confound explicitly and in the language the review needs: without a shared vocabulary for scaffold design, researchers cannot attribute observed differences to specific architectural choices, and the confound between scaffold design and model capability goes unacknowledged. It also documents the concrete mechanism by which prior work fails, citing trajectory studies that compared Claude 3.5 Sonnet-based OpenHands against DeepSeek-V3-based Prometheus, making scaffold and model effects inseparable. Its most useful contribution for RQ2 is a refusal: the author deliberately declines to benchmark, on the stated grounds that SWE-bench results across agents are not comparable because different agents used different underlying models and model capability is a larger confounder than scaffold design. In place of measurement it supplies the variable list a controlled experiment would need, proposing comparisons with identical tool sets but different loop strategies, or identical loops but different compaction strategies, with the model held constant. It also cites a controlled result worth following up, that prompt interventions adding or removing testing under a minimal scaffold change outcomes by at most 2.6 percentage points, suggesting scaffold-level orchestration rather than model-native behaviour is the relevant variable.

quotes.text:
First, without a shared vocabulary for scaffold design,
researchers studying agent behavior cannot attribute observed differences to specific architectural
choices; the confound between scaffold design and model capability goes unacknowledged.

As noted in Section 3.5, SWE-bench comparisons between agents confound scaffold design, model
choice, and configuration in a single metric.

finding that prompt interventions that add or remove testing change outcomes
by at most 2.6 percentage points

extraction.topology: fixed pipeline (Agentless), user-driven loop (Aider), sequential ReAct loop (7 of 13), phased loop (AutoCodeRover, Prometheus), depth-first tree search (DARS-Agent) and full MCTS (Moatless Tools)
extraction.key_results: Source-code taxonomy of 13 open-source coding agent scaffolds analysed at pinned commit hashes across 12 dimensions in three layers. Control strategies range from fixed pipelines with no feedback to full MCTS with reward backpropagation; LLM-callable tool counts range from 0 (Aider) to 37 action classes (Moatless Tools); context compaction spans seven distinct strategies; state management ranges from destructive overwrite to event sourcing. Five loop primitives compose freely and 11 of 13 agents layer multiple primitives rather than using a single control structure, while 7 of 13 use a sequential ReAct loop as the primary control structure. Exact-string replacement editing appears independently in 5 of 13 agents, and 5 of 13 support explicit sub-agent spawning through five distinct mechanisms. A post-hoc verification pass over 296 extracted claims confirmed 267, corrected 19 and accepted 10 as minor simplifications.
extraction.limitations: Single-author analysis with LLM-assisted code navigation and self-verification rather than independent review, so classification judgements reflect one interpretation. The nine pilot dimensions may not have surfaced all relevant axes, and prompt engineering strategy was deliberately excluded as a dimension even though the authors call it an important aspect of scaffold design. The taxonomy is a snapshot at pinned commits, and dimensions are presented as independent axes although several are acknowledged to be correlated. The corpus covers only open-source, source-inspectable, largely Python and SWE-bench-oriented agents, giving survivorship bias and analytical rather than statistical generalizability. Static source analysis misses runtime behaviour, and no performance benchmarking was conducted.

records.title: The Necessity of a Unified Framework for LLM-Based Agent Evaluation

evidence_notes.summary: This is the methodological backbone for RQ2 in the assignment set: it argues that whether a harness must be held constant is not a universal rule but a function of the declared candidate boundary, so fixing the scaffold is required for model-level claims, optional for agent-system claims, and deliberately relaxed for robustness claims. It supplies a checklist of exactly the harness components RQ1 names, treating prompt scaffolding, planning strategy, memory serialization and compaction, tool schema translation, and parsing and retry or repair policy as factors that must be fixed or semantically matched before any score difference can be attributed to the model. Its most consequential caveat for the review is that a fixed reference harness does not deliver a harness-independent capability estimate, only a conditional one, and that the reference harness is not neutral and may interact differently with different model families, which means a single locked harness cannot fully answer RQ1 either. The paper explicitly positions itself as agnostic on whether model or harness variance dominates, so it should be cited for design guidance rather than for magnitude. Note that the retrieved full text is a later version titled 'LLM Agent Performance Is Not a Single Evaluation Target', which differs from the ledger title.

quotes.text:
LLM agent benchmark scores are shaped not
only by the model but also by the agent harness,
environment, evaluator, and inference budget.

Small
differences in this stack can redirect subsequent
actions and observations, altering both absolute
scores and model rankings

A reference harness is not neutral
and may interact differently with different model
families.

extraction.topology: n/a
extraction.key_results: No new measurements. The paper argues that 'LLM agent performance' is an umbrella term rather than a single evaluation target, and derives four comparison classes from two design decisions: the candidate boundary (an LLM evaluated through a reference stack versus a complete agent system) and the condition policy (factors outside the boundary held at reference values, semantically matched, or systematically varied), with robustness cutting across both. It enumerates the non-model sources of variation that must be fixed or matched for model-level attribution, including inference interface and engine, prompt and planning scaffold, memory serialization and compaction policy, tool schema translation and validation, parsing and retry or repair policy, and environment. It specifies minimum reporting requirements (candidate boundary, which components were fixed, candidate-owned or varied, harness and evaluator versions, budgets, retry policies, aggregation, uncertainty) and recommends separate leaderboard tracks with anchor-candidate bridge evaluations across benchmark revisions.
extraction.limitations: The position isolates how candidate boundaries and condition policies constrain comparative attribution and does not resolve task-construct validity, evaluator bias, benchmark contamination or statistical adequacy. A reference harness is not neutral and may interact differently with different model families. Compatibility between condition policies remains domain-dependent, no finite perturbation set establishes robustness to all deployment settings, and extension to embodied or safety-focused evaluation requires further study.

records.title: Benchmarking Reference-Free LLM Agent Robustness Under Schema, Policy, and Toolset Drift

evidence_notes.summary: This is the most rigorously controlled study in the assignment set and the one that most directly probes RQ1's harness components, since its treatments are exactly a repair-rule layer, a memory-hint layer and a schema-normalization layer applied over an otherwise identical base LLM call at temperature 0. Its central finding is a warning against assuming harness additions help: a memory or replay layer significantly degraded task success for four of five models, with a fitted odds ratio of 0.554, while the rules layer helped only two of five. That makes harness effects model-conditional rather than additive, which complicates any single attribution estimate. It also gives a clean decomposition of model versus harness variance in the same table, since static baselines under an identical harness span 0.130 to 0.432 across models while controller changes shift a given model by at most about 9 points. The schema-obedience result is a useful mechanism finding: the normalization layer was load-bearing only for the model that faithfully called the drifted tool names, while models falling back on training-time tool knowledge were unaffected and also unresponsive to intentional schema updates. Statistical practice is strong, with paired McNemar tests, Wilson intervals and an explicit power calculation, and the authors state eleven limitations.

quotes.text:
Blind replay consistently degrades reference-free task success
relative to static for four of five models; Kimi K2 is the exception, for which both blind replay and rules-only
significantly improve over the static baseline.

Controller stack. Three reference-free controller condi-
tions share the same base LLM call and differ only in which
repair stages are active at each step.

Removing normalization reduces GPT-4o mini
from 0.396 to 0.322 overall

extraction.topology: single-agent tool-calling loop with a deterministic bijective drift-inversion normalization layer and three controller variants (static, rules-only, blind replay) under a 12-step budget
extraction.benchmark: tau2-bench retail domain, 10 train and 30 disjoint eval scenarios by 3 episodes by 3 drift families, giving up to 270 trials per model-condition cell
extraction.baseline: The static controller for each model (bare LLM call with no memory cue and no repair rules), plus a reference-guided exact-trajectory replay condition reported only as an incommensurable upper bound
extraction.key_results: Reference-guided replay reaches 0.7083 task success over 216 trials for GPT-4o mini (95% CI 0.6428-0.7680), but that advantage does not transfer to the reference-free regime. Reference-free static baselines span 0.130 (Kimi K2) to 0.432 (Qwen3-32B) across five models under an identical harness. Blind replay significantly degrades success relative to static for four of five models (GPT-4o mini chi-square 28.12 p<0.001, GPT-4o 29.09 p<0.001, DeepSeek V3 7.69 p=0.006, Qwen3-32B 33.44 p<0.001) but improves Kimi K2 (10.24, p=0.001, 0.193 vs 0.130). Rules-only is model-dependent, improving Kimi K2 (0.211 vs 0.130, p<0.001) and Qwen3-32B (0.526 vs 0.432, p=0.007), non-significant for GPT-4o and DeepSeek V3, and borderline negative for GPT-4o mini (0.352 vs 0.396, p=0.052). Logistic regression gives blind replay beta = -0.591 (OR 0.554) and rules-only beta = +0.133 (OR 1.142). Removing the normalization layer drops GPT-4o mini from 0.396 to 0.322 with 30 toolset-drift episodes terminating early, an asymmetry absent for the other four models. Per-drift-family spread is small, for example 0.344-0.433 for GPT-4o mini, and invalid tool-call rates are effectively zero.
extraction.limitations: Eleven numbered limitations: the three drift types are a narrow controlled slice of real interface drift; all tasks are tau2 retail so external validity is unestablished; individual pairwise comparisons at small effect sizes remain underpowered at n=270 per cell; only three controllers were compared, omitting multi-step memory cues, observation-based argument repair and planning-augmented disambiguation; the upper-bound and reference-free evaluators are incommensurable by design; the bijective normalization layer defers the drift-detection subproblem; token cost and latency were not instrumented; OpenRouter providers may silently update weights so exact reproduction is not guaranteed; Anthropic frontier models are omitted; within-episode error-driven adaptation was not evaluated; and no principled reference-free progress metric was implemented.
extraction.varied_factor: model, memory (replay hint), retry-policy (deterministic repair rules), and tool-schema through injected schema, policy and toolset drift

records.title: Schema First Tool APIs for LLM Agents: A Controlled Study of Tool Misuse, Recovery, and Budgeted Performance

evidence_notes.summary: This pilot is methodologically the cleanest single-factor manipulation of a harness component in the set, since the agent loop, system prompt, formatting constraints, tool availability, sandbox artifacts, decoding parameters, tool semantics and runtime error messages are all held constant and only the tool interface representation and validation-diagnostic format change, with information equivalence enforced by generating prose and JSON Schema from one canonical contract. That design is a direct template for the controlled experiment RQ1 implies. Its results, however, are largely null: task success is 0.0 in every condition and every budget, so the schema manipulation cannot be shown to affect end-task performance at all. What it does show is a decomposition worth carrying forward, namely that schema conditions cut interface misuse from 5.39 to 3.72 mean invalid calls and eliminate execution failures, while semantic misuse rises from 0.93 to 3.03, implying the harness moved the failure mode rather than removing it. The severe confound is capability floor: a quantized 0.5B model with three seeds cannot support any claim about how much of a performance difference is harness-attributable, and the authors scope their claims accordingly.

quotes.text:
In this pilot, success
remains zero across conditions, while schema conditions reduce interface misuse but not semantic
misuse.

To isolate interface effects, we hold constant the agent loop and
prompting across conditions like the system prompt, formatting constraints, tool availability, sandbox
artifacts, and decoding parameters.

Relative to prose (A), schema conditions (B/C) show lower average interface misuse (mean invalid
calls: A = 5.39, B = 3.72, C = 3.72 over all budgets), consistent with directional support for H1
at the misuse level.

extraction.topology: single-agent budgeted tool-calling loop at step budgets of 3, 5, 8 and 12
extraction.benchmark: Custom deterministic software-engineering diagnostic sandbox, an 8-task reduced pack spanning logs, metrics, configuration files and a small repository with tests
extraction.baseline: Condition A, free-form natural-language tool documentation generated from the same canonical tool contract as the schema conditions, enforcing information equivalence
extraction.key_results: A one-model pilot (Qwen2.5 0.5B Instruct, quantized), three seeds, three interface conditions and four budgets produced 276 scored runs, 2,208 step records and 12 exclusions from infrastructure timeouts concentrated in one repository-debug task family. Task success was 0.0 across all conditions and all budgets, so the predeclared primary endpoint (tight-budget success at B in {3,5}) is uninformative and paired success tests return null effects. Mean invalid calls fell from 5.39 under prose to 3.72 under both schema conditions, and mean execution failures from 0.54 to 0.00, but mean semantic misuse rose from 0.93 to 3.03. Invalid and semantic misuse counts increased monotonically with budget in all conditions without any corresponding success gain.
extraction.limitations: The authors state four threats to validity plus a claim-scope restriction: representation parity between prose and schema conditions, mitigated by generating both from one canonical contract; model scope, since results come from one small local model and are explicitly scoped to it; oracle overconstraint, since semantic-misuse labelling may penalise valid alternative strategies; and external validity of synthetic tasks. They further concede that zero end-to-end success makes the primary endpoint uninformative, that all 12 exclusions were infrastructure timeouts in a single task family indicating an operational bottleneck, and that claims are scoped to diagnostic reliability characterisation in a one-model, three-seed pilot.
extraction.varied_factor: tool-schema, specifically the tool interface representation and the validation-diagnostic format

records.title: Five Whys as an Epistemic-Honesty Scaffold for Multi-Agent LLM Analysis of Industrial Time Series

evidence_notes.summary: This is one of the cleanest harness-isolation designs in the batch: the same multi-agent system, the same seed, the same Domain prefix and the same shared synthesis procedure are held fixed, and the single manipulated factor is whether a data-blind reviewer scaffold is present. The authors additionally equalise analysis depth across arms explicitly to remove trajectory length as a confound, which is the exact confound RQ1 targets. The result is that a scaffold change alone flips the system's headline output from a confident but unverified root cause to an honest abstention, without any change of model, tools or data. The paper also bounds the scaffold's contribution by capability tier: the strongest model reaches the honest verdict unaided, so the measured scaffold effect exists only in an intermediate capability band, which is direct evidence that scaffold and model effects interact rather than add. Against RQ2 it is a positive case that nonetheless under-reports the harness, since sampling parameters, context limits and retry behaviour are explicitly withheld.

quotes.text: We treat the MAS architecture as fixed across all conditions; the only manipulated factor is the presence or absence of the reviewer.
the comparison is between an MAS that analyses to the same depth with and without the Five Whys discipline, not between a longer and a shorter run.

We report model identifiers, seeds, chain count, and round budget, and give the operator in Appendix A, but not full API-level configuration such as sampling parameters, context limits, and retry behaviour, on which LLM outputs can depend.

extraction.topology: pipeline (Domain, Strategy, Analysis, Claim-Graph, Synthesis agents) with a toggled data-blind Five Whys reviewer overlay
extraction.benchmark: public AirPassengers monthly series (in-data root) and a non-public industrial power-consumption series (exogenous root)
extraction.baseline: the identical MAS run without the reviewer, from the same Domain prefix and the same random seed, and run to the same number of analysis steps (matched depth)
extraction.key_results: Three-seed mean contested-claim count on the industrial series rises with the reviewer for all three capable-MAS pairings: haiku x opus 5.3 -> 9.7, opus x haiku 15.0 -> 19.7, haiku x haiku 10.3 -> 13.0; the top-tier peer pairing (opus x opus) is per-seed identical (9.3 = 9.3); on the benchmark series the count falls in all three seeds (7.0 -> 3.7). Per-seed counts are highly variable and individual seeds reverse sign. Qualitatively, one Five Whys chain drove the MAS to test and retract three grounded-sounding mechanisms and abstain, while the matched baseline committed to one as a confident but unverified cause.
extraction.limitations: Primary evidence is qualitative by design; the importance metric is distorted by causal cycles in about forty per cent of cells and is excluded from all claims; the three metrics are operationalisations rather than validated instruments; the contestation effect is a mean-level effect with large per-seed variance and occasional sign reversals; ground truth on the industrial series is unconfirmable and that dataset is non-public so it cannot be independently replicated; only two datasets, one Five Whys chain and three seeds; the regime contrast confounds root locus with dataset complexity and pre-training familiarity; analyst-reviewer pairs are all within one model family; no ablation of the reviewer prompt itself; full API-level configuration including sampling parameters, context limits and retry behaviour is not reported.

records.title: Agentic AI Between Capability and Reliability: A Structured Review of Architectures, Design Patterns, Evaluation Practice, and Enterprise Deployment

evidence_notes.summary: Screened core from the abstract, but no full text could be retrieved with the institutional session; recorded as an explicit evidence gap rather than relabelled to let the stopping rule pass.

records.title: A Comparative Empirical Evaluation of Single-Agent and Multi-Agent LLM Prompting Strategies for Automated Formative Feedback in Education

evidence_notes.summary: This study frames itself as isolating architecture, and it does hold the model, decoding settings and rubric constant across the four conditions, explicitly claiming that shared instructional framing lets quality differences be attributed to architectural and prompting variation. But the design confounds exactly the two things RQ1 separates: moving from S2 to S3 to S4 adds agent roles and simultaneously adds chain-of-thought, role-playing and rubric-guided prompting, so the reported single-agent versus multi-agent gap cannot be attributed to topology alone. Nothing is reported about tool schemas, retry policy or orchestration failure handling beyond a custom message-passing pipeline, so the harness is only partly pinned. It is useful for RQ2 as a case where the authors believe they held the harness constant while the varied factor is in fact a bundle of scaffold changes, and where the cost axis (4.6x tokens for the top configuration) shows the price of the extra scaffolding.

quotes.text: These principles were embedded into the prompt templates for all four strategies, ensuring that observed quality differences could be attributed to architectural and prompting variations rather than inconsistencies in instructional framing.
A one -way repeated -measures ANOVA confirmed a statistically significant main effect of prompting strategy on CQS, F(3, 597) = 47.32, p < 0.001, partial eta -squared = 0.19.
The most striking finding is the monotonic decrease in error rates as architectural complexity increases.

extraction.topology: four configurations: zero-shot single-agent (S1), chain-of-thought single-agent (S2), dual-agent Evaluator-Reviewer pipeline (S3), tri-agent Evaluator-Student Simulator-Reviewer pipeline (S4)
extraction.benchmark: a corpus of 200 undergraduate argumentative essays pre-scored by the course instructor; automated metrics BERTScore F1, ROUGE-L and BLEU-4 against instructor reference feedback for a 40-essay subset
extraction.baseline: the zero-shot single-agent configuration S1, with the chain-of-thought single-agent S2 as a second reference point
extraction.key_results: Composite Quality Score: S4 = 4.21, S3 = 3.89, S2 = 3.64, S1 = 3.11 on a five-point scale; one-way repeated-measures ANOVA F(3, 597) = 47.32, p < 0.001, partial eta-squared = 0.19. At least one error type occurred in 84.0% of S1 outputs versus 27.0% of S4 outputs; over-praise 63.5% -> 15.5%, hallucination 21.5% -> 4.0%. BERTScore F1 0.594 (S1) to 0.673 (S4). Mean token consumption per instance 847 / 1,264 / 2,531 / 3,892 for S1-S4, so S2 reaches 86.5% of S4's CQS at 32.5% of its token cost.
extraction.limitations: The authors state that the study used a single LLM (GPT-4-Turbo) so cross-model generalisability is unestablished; the corpus comes from a single institution and a single discipline; only three human raters were used; feedback quality was evaluated as a static property of one interaction with no longitudinal or learner-outcome measurement.

records.title: Benchmarking LLM Judges for Mobile Agent Evaluation

evidence_notes.summary: This is a fully crossed 6 methods x 5 backends design, which makes it one of the few studies in the batch that can actually decompose how much of a reported difference belongs to the pipeline versus the model. Its central RQ1 finding is that among competitive methods the backbone explains far more accuracy variance than the judge pipeline (11% method versus 49% backbone once the two weakest purpose-built methods are dropped), and that a minimal baseline judge matches or beats elaborate purpose-built pipelines. The ablations further show that most of the elaborate scaffolding inputs, UI metadata and agent reasoning traces, contribute at most a couple of points while a single configuration variable (screenshot count) dominates. The reinforcement-learning arm is a clean harness-held-constant comparison: all conditions share identical hyperparameters and only the reward source differs. The paper also demonstrates the downstream cost of an uncontrolled evaluation harness, since judge choice alone shifts agent rankings by up to 13 positions.

quotes.text: A two-way variance decomposition over the 6×5 grid quantifies the two factors: method choice explains 49% of the accuracy variance and the backbone 21%, but the method share is driven by the two weakest methods, both purpose-built (the A3 modes).
All conditions share identical hyperparameters; only the reward source differs.

Once those are excluded, backbone choice explains most of the remaining variance (Appendix D.4); among competitive methods, upgrading the backbone yields greater returns than engineering elaborate judge prompts.

extraction.framework: MobileJudgeBench
extraction.topology: n/a (judge methods scoring trajectories produced by four mobile agents)
extraction.benchmark: MobileJudgeBench: 931 human-annotated trajectories drawn from SPA-Bench, AndroidWorld, A3, AndroidArena, B-MoCA and AndroidLab across 289 tasks and 68 apps
extraction.baseline: a deliberately simple baseline judge designed for controlled ablation; human expert labels as ground truth; a rule-based oracle checker in the reinforcement-learning study
extraction.key_results: Judge accuracy spans 76.4-90.9% across 30 method x backend variants; the simple baseline leads on Gemini (90.9%), GPT-5-mini (90.8%) and Qwen (85.7%) while AgentRewardBench leads on GLM (86.1%) and Claude (87.2%). The same method varies 5.6-10.5pp across backends. A two-way variance decomposition attributes 49% of accuracy variance to method and 21% to backbone, but excluding the two weakest (purpose-built) methods reverses the shares to 11% versus 49%. Ablations: screenshot count dominates, UI metadata changes accuracy by at most 0.3pp and agent reasoning by about 1.7pp. F1 predicts agent ranking fidelity best (rho_s = 0.90), balanced accuracy predicts rate-estimation error best (rho_s = -0.79), precision is non-predictive (rho_s = 0.00, CI [-0.23, 0.30]). In on-policy GRPO training with identical hyperparameters, best easy-set success rate tracks judge accuracy: rule-based 54.6%, GPT-5-mini 45.4%, GPT-5.2 42.6%, Qwen 39.9%.
extraction.limitations: The authors note the benchmark covers only binary success/failure judgments, leaving optimality, efficiency and partial progress to future work; the training experiments use a single environment (AndroidWorld) and a single judge method, so training-time comparisons are narrower than the offline study; the root-cause classification involves subjective judgment in borderline cases; the equal-accuracy precision comparison depends on a best-checkpoint convention and ties at the fixed final checkpoint, so it is reported as suggestive rather than conclusive.

records.title: Harness Resilience: From LLM Availability to Toolchain Continuity in Agentic AI Engineering

evidence_notes.summary: This paper contributes the definitional and vocabulary layer that RQ1 needs rather than any measurement. It draws an explicit operational boundary between the model, the harness (planning loop, context assembly, tool exposure, permissions, approvals, traces, fallback routing) and the application, and argues that the practical unit of dependency is the model-harness combination rather than the model. Its boundary-contract checklist gives four concrete tests for whether a component is harness-critical (does replacing it change tool authorization, context assembly, state mutation, or audit evidence), which is directly usable as a coding scheme for classifying what counts as a harness change in other studies. It also proposes a minimum provenance trace schema requiring model and harness version, feature flags, prompt-policy version and context-compression module to be recorded before every model call, which is exactly the reporting that RQ2 finds missing elsewhere. It supplies no empirical estimate of harness attribution: the only numbers in the paper are explicitly labelled a synthetic example of metric reporting.

quotes.text: Increasingly, productivity depends on an execution harness: the surrounding runtime of prompts, tools, sandboxes, permissions, memory, repositories, connectors, model-routing policies, observability, and user-interface affordances that turn a model into an operational coding or general-purpose agent.
The practical unit of dependency is no longer “the model” but the model-harness combination.

This paper is primarily a position paper and practice framework. It does not yet report a controlled empirical study, multi-organization case evidence, or statistically powered comparison of harnesses.

extraction.topology: n/a (proposes a four-layer reference architecture: model provider, agent harness, application, governance)
extraction.limitations: The author states the paper is primarily a position paper and practice framework, that it does not report a controlled empirical study, multi-organization case evidence or a statistically powered comparison of harnesses, and that the proposed KPIs and evaluation plan require calibration in real engineering environments.

records.title: RefactorBench-JS: Evaluating LLM Agents on Behavior-Preserving Code Decomposition

evidence_notes.summary: This is the strongest direct evidence in the batch for RQ1, because it varies exactly one harness component while pinning everything else: same 123 fixtures, temperature 0, tool_choice required, a 50 tool-call cap, up to 3 retries with fresh conversation state, and the same system prompt, with only the test-runner tool toggled. The result is that the same tool is worth +9.8pp for one model and -2.4pp for another, so tool augmentation effects are model-dependent and a model ranking taken under one tool configuration does not transfer to another. It also quantifies the harness's role in evaluation validity: agents report success on 49-84% of runs that fail behavioural tests, and the dominant failure buckets are completion, reporting and syntax rather than subtle behavioural drift, meaning much of what looks like model capability is really scaffold completion behaviour. Notably the authors withhold the production agent harness and system prompts from the public release, so the benchmark is reproducible only if a user supplies their own harness, which is itself an RQ2 reproducibility limit. The paper explicitly recommends that model and tool choices be evaluated jointly rather than independently.

quotes.text: All agents use temperature 0,tool_choice=required, a maximum of 50 tool calls per attempt, and up to 3 retry attempts with fresh conversation state.
Because every condition runs onthe same fixtures, file complexity is controlled by design.
This interaction effect—the same tool helping some models while not helping others—is a central empirical finding.

extraction.framework: RefactorBench-JS
extraction.topology: single-agent multi-turn tool-calling refactoring agent, deployed in production as a subagent invoked by a base code-generation agent
extraction.benchmark: RefactorBench-JS: 123 scored JavaScript/React fixtures, each paired with a hidden holdout unit-test suite executed against the refactored filesystem
extraction.baseline: paired within-model comparison of the test-runner tool enabled versus disabled on the identical fixture set, plus agent self-reported success as a contrast to hidden-test pass
extraction.key_results: 7 models x 2 tool configurations on the same 123 fixtures. Hidden-test pass rates range 10.6% to 25.2% (Gemini 3.0 Pro with test runner highest at 25.2%, Sonnet 4.6 with test runner 23.6%). Paired exact McNemar tests on the test-runner effect: Sonnet 4.6 +9.8pp (p = 0.0018), Opus 4.6 +5.7pp (p = 0.0391), Gemini 3.0 Pro +7.3pp (p = 0.0039), Opus 4.7 +0.8pp (p = 1.0000), Gemini 2.0 Flash -2.4pp, Gemini 2.5 Pro -0.8pp. False-confidence rate (reported success that fails hidden tests) 49.1% to 83.5%. 86 of 123 fixtures passed in zero of 14 conditions; zero-pass targets average 1,294 lines versus 372 for fixtures that passed at least once. Aggregate error buckets over 1,436 failed outcomes: 47.9% reported non-success, 29.4% syntax or parse failure, 15.3% module import/export failure. Production success rate moved from about 65% to above 97%, reported as observational rather than causal.
extraction.limitations: The author states the corpus is JavaScript/React-focused and drawn from a single production context so domain bias is possible; hidden tests are public in the released repository, creating future contamination risk; only two tool configurations are evaluated, with no full tool ablation; the iterative-versus-batch tool-calling behavioural claims are qualitative and unquantified; hidden test suites vary in authorship and coverage; the production improvement was deployed incrementally without A/B testing and confounded with other engineering changes.

records.title: Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents

evidence_notes.summary: This paper isolates a prompt-level harness change with unusual precision: UAM and the proposed method differ only by the addition of one uncertainty field and its explanation, and the authors attribute the resulting 0.8 percentage-point success-rate drop directly to the enlarged prompt rather than to any architectural change. That is a clean, if small, measurement of harness cost, and it generalises into the claim they call capability dilution: each additional instrumentation objective added to the prompt degrades the primary task objective because they share a fixed reasoning budget. The paper is even more directly useful for RQ1 through its aggregation analysis, which shows that a practitioner tuning only the trajectory-level aggregation function can produce arbitrarily large apparent differences between methods without changing the underlying signal at all, and that high product-aggregation ROC-AUC on ALFWorld reflects trajectory length rather than confidence quality. Both findings are instances of a harness or scoring choice masquerading as a method effect. Comparisons hold benchmarks, backbones and run counts fixed across the three methods.

quotes.text: The monotonic drop from UAM (27.8%) to the proposed method (27.0%) isolates this effect
In practice this means a practitioner tuning only the aggregation can produce arbitrarily large differences between methods without changing the underlying uncertainty signal.

The qualitative takeaway is that high product-aggregation ROC-AUC should not be interpreted as evidence that the confidence signal is informative; it can simply be evidence that the agent took more steps to fail.

extraction.topology: single-agent ReAct-style think-act-observe loop with prompt-level uncertainty instrumentation and deterministic clarification routing
extraction.benchmark: WebShop, ALFWorld and REAL for fault detection, plus two clarification-augmented variants (WebShop-Clarification, ALFWorld-Clarification) in which 50% of tasks are deliberately underspecified; 100 tasks per method-benchmark pair
extraction.baseline: ReAct with an uncertainty-estimation prompt suffix (ReAct+UE) and Uncertainty-Aware Memory (UAM), both prompt-based and both prior work
extraction.key_results: Averaged over five backbones the proposed decomposition improves clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification by 73% over ReAct+UE and 36% over UAM, leading on every backbone on WebShop-Clarification and four of five on ALFWorld-Clarification (about +0.28 absolute F1 over ReAct+UE and +0.21 over UAM). Mean task success rate falls monotonically with added instrumentation: 28.6% (ReAct+UE) to 27.8% (UAM) to 27.0% (proposed), with the degradation concentrated on REAL (32.1% to 19.2%) and WebShop (31.9% to 26.1%) and absent on ALFWorld. All methods are systematically overconfident with per-panel ECE 0.24 to 0.66. Replacing real per-step confidences with i.i.d. U(0,1) draws or a deterministic 1/length score matches or exceeds the real product-aggregation ROC-AUC on ALFWorld (0.92-0.99), showing that aggregation acts as a trajectory-length proxy.
extraction.limitations: The author states three limitations of the prompt-based paradigm: adding uncertainty instructions consistently degrades task-solving ability (capability dilution, attributed to a fixed shared reasoning budget rather than phrasing); all methods show systematic overconfidence; and trajectory-level aggregation introduces a consequential hyperparameter whose product variant can act as a length proxy rather than a confidence signal. Also noted: the clarification benchmarks rely on synthetic, procedurally generated underspecification and score clarification as a single binary action.

records.title: Causal Agent Replay: Counterfactual Attribution for LLM-Agent Failures

evidence_notes.summary: CAR supplies the methodological machinery RQ1 needs: it treats an agent run as a structural causal model and attributes outcome change to a specific step by intervening on that step while holding the rest of the run at its factual values, then re-executing under the same stochastic policy. Its five do-operations map neatly onto harness components (do_context edits the assembled history, do_policy swaps the model from a step onward, do_observation replaces a tool result), so the same algebra could in principle be used to attribute an outcome difference to scaffold versus model. Two findings matter for confounding. First, provider nondeterminism means a faithful replay cannot be assumed even at temperature 0, so the paper reports an action-match rate instead of claiming reproducibility, and frames every effect as a distribution with confidence intervals. Second, resampling one step re-rolls every downstream stochastic step, so an irrelevant early step appears causally influential purely through downstream re-rolling, and magnitude alone cannot localise the cause: this is precisely the class of attribution error that naive harness-versus-model comparisons would make. Validation is on synthetic SCMs with known ground truth rather than on real agent workloads.

quotes.text: Providers are not deterministic. Even at temperature0, hosted inference varies because of floating-point non-associativity and batch-size-dependent kernels [11]; and current frontier models may not accept a temperature parameter at all.
Magnitude alone cannot localize the cause.

The contrastive effect is a total effect through a stochastic continuation; isolating a step's direct effect calls for common random numbers across branches, which is hard across divergent LLM contexts and is left as a refinement.

extraction.framework: Causal Agent Replay (CAR)
extraction.topology: single-agent trajectory modelled as a structural causal model over steps; demonstrated on a customer-support agent absorbing a prompt injection
extraction.benchmark: synthetic structural causal models with planted ground truth shipped as regression tests; the Who&When failure-attribution benchmark is cited as context
extraction.baseline: LLM-judge step-level attribution on Who&When (best reported accuracy about 14%); the contrastive single-step estimator and the Monte-Carlo Shapley estimator are also compared against each other
extraction.key_results: On a three-step SCM with a pivotal middle step the contrastive estimator recovers the locus and downstream resampling shows no significant effect. On an AND-failure SCM the Shapley estimator recovers phi_0 = 0.44, phi_1 = 0.45, phi_2 approximately 0, with an efficiency sum of 0.909 against the analytic 0.91, while the contrastive estimator over-counts on the same run. A single-stream local model with a fixed seed replays exactly; hosted providers do not, so CAR reports an action-match rate rather than asserting reproducibility.
extraction.limitations: The author states the contrastive effect is a total effect through a stochastic continuation and isolating a direct effect would need common random numbers across branches, which is hard across divergent LLM contexts; judge-based outcome functions inject their own noise so rule-based outcomes are preferred; real tools with side effects are out of scope and the demonstrations use mocked reproducible tools; Shapley is exponential in the worst case and the variance-versus-budget tradeoff is real.

records.title: Benchmarking LLM Judges for Voice-Agent Evaluation: Reliability, Calibration, and Human Oversight

evidence_notes.summary: The design explicitly tests whether automated judgments are sensitive to the evaluation setup by scoring the same interactions under three configurations (no persona, static persona injection, dynamically inferred context) and two judge models, with identical rubric definitions and an identical aggregation procedure supplied to humans and judges. The headline RQ1-relevant result is a partial dissociation: changing the evaluator model or the prompting configuration has minimal impact on the direction and relative ordering of metric scores, but a large impact on absolute calibration, and the size of that miscalibration is domain-dependent rather than uniform. That matters because a study that reports absolute scores from an LLM judge is reporting a quantity that moves with the evaluation harness, while rank-order comparisons are more robust. The paper is only partially harness-controlled for the agent itself: p1 and p2 change what context the agent under evaluation receives, so agent behaviour and judge behaviour vary together across configurations. It also documents that no single judge model is uniformly best, with alignment shifting by metric, which argues against treating any one judge configuration as a neutral measuring instrument.

quotes.text: The same interactions are scored under three evaluation configurations, p0, p1, and p2, to test whether automated judgments are sensitive to the evaluation setup and whether observed patterns generalize across configurations and judge models.

The results indicate that changes in evaluator model or prompting strategy have minimal impact on overall metric behavior, with the primary difference lying in score calibration rather than evaluation direction.
Neither GPT-4.1 nor GPT-5 consistently leads the other in agreement with human judgment. Instead, alignment shifts by metric.

extraction.topology: n/a (human evaluators and LLM judges scoring the same voice-agent conversations)
extraction.benchmark: a proprietary set of 242 retail and telecom voice-agent conversations across six configurations (p0, p1, p2 in each domain); metric definitions and rubrics adopted unchanged from the companion MM-tau-p2 benchmark
extraction.baseline: human expert judgment, three trained annotators per telecom conversation with adjudication by a fourth senior annotator
extraction.key_results: Human-to-LLM score ratios stay near 1 for Turn Efficiency and Confirmation Recall in both domains, but safety metrics diverge sharply: Irreversible Action Safety 4.03-6.08 and Safety Recall 3.07-5.64 in telecom versus 1.19-1.75 and 1.06-1.63 in retail. ASR-Robust Goal Achievement sits below 1 throughout (0.117-0.265 telecom, 0.383-0.657 retail), so judges score recovery more leniently than humans. Recovery Turn Count is the most volatile metric (1.889-6.064 telecom). Human-autoeval cross-metric correlation is strong in retail (r = 0.912 for GPT-4.1, r = 0.943 for GPT-5) but weak in telecom and not statistically significant for GPT-4.1 (r = 0.295, p = 0.408 at N = 10). Neither judge model is uniformly closer to human judgment.
extraction.limitations: The authors state the benchmark does not model temporal and interaction-level phenomena unique to voice (missed response windows, silence, interruptions, overtalk, barge-in) because these are hard to capture from text transcripts alone; the proposed calibration framework needs validation across larger datasets, more tasks and more diverse speakers and acoustic conditions; rubrics for safety-sensitive escalation and multi-turn recovery need refinement.

records.title: AgentFairBench: Do LLM Agents Discriminate When They Act?

evidence_notes.summary: AgentFairBench treats scaffold depth as a first-class experimental variable rather than an implementation detail, running the identical counterfactual matched sets through four rungs of increasing agency and holding profile content constant so any measured difference is attributable to the manipulated factor. That design is a direct template for RQ1: it asks whether adding chain-of-thought, deliberation or tool use amplifies an entering effect, and it reports the honest null that no amplification survives the correct noise floor. The methodological finding is the most transferable part for this review: comparing a six-group spread against a two-run pairwise difference inflates the apparent effect by roughly 2.4x through statistic arity alone, and the authors show earlier drafts of their own work read that artifact as signal. The lesson generalises to harness comparisons, where a scaffold that produces more variation across conditions can look like a real effect unless benchmarked against a matched-arity null. The pilot also documents an 8% decision flip rate on pure resampling at default temperature, which bounds how small a harness effect can be credibly detected without pinning decoding.

quotes.text: Scaffolding complexity is a first-class variable in AgentFairBench, reflecting BCF Proposition P3 (super-additivity) and the claim that agentic structure can amplify or attenuate bias introduced at any component.
That comparison is wrong, and correcting it is the central methodological lesson of the pilot.
But after the arity correction of Finding 1, every one of these values is below its own noise floor

extraction.framework: AgentFairBench (operationalising the companion Bias Conduction Framework, BCF)
extraction.topology: a four-rung scaffold ladder: C0 direct prompt, C2 chain-of-thought, C3 two-agent reviewer-then-decision pipeline, C4 tool-augmented information gathering
extraction.benchmark: AgentFairBench across hiring, lending and medical triage, with synthetic demographic-neutral profiles in counterfactual matched sets varying only a name-coded race x gender signal
extraction.baseline: a white-male reference group, a test-retest noise floor from a second independent run, an arity-matched six-group noise spread, and a BiasedMock planted-bias property test
extraction.key_results: 864 decisions plus a 648-decision retest run on claude-haiku-4-5. Test-retest decision agreement 0.917 and per-cell score MAE 0.15-5.75. Comparing the six-group MASD spread to the two-run pairwise noise floor gives ratios of 1.24-3.33x (mean about 2.4x); against an arity-matched six-group noise spread every C0-C3 cell falls below 1.0 (mean 0.83). Raw MASD rises across the scaffold ladder in hiring (7.83, 8.83, 12.17) and triage (0.42, 0.75, 0.83) but not lending, and all values sit below their own noise floor. Zero of 120 pairwise contrasts and zero of nine omnibus ANOVA group tests survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction (minimum uncorrected p = 0.072 and 0.082). Largest tool-invocation disparity is 0.25 in hiring on counts of 3, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0 of 12. Full run costs $1.79.
extraction.limitations: The authors state the pilot is a single model at 12 matched sets per cell and is underpowered for cell-level significance; version 1 does not pin sampling temperature; the second-run raw scores were not committed as a separate trace file so the arity-matched null is estimated from the primary run's residual rather than a true repeated-measurement design, and there is no interval on the floor itself; binary decision metrics saturate; only single-turn domains are covered, with multi-step tool use, episodic memory and long-horizon trajectories not yet instrumented; name-coding conflates familiarity, cultural context and perceived ethnicity.

records.title: RecoAtlas: From Semantic Plausibility to Set-Level Utility in LLM Recommendation Agents

evidence_notes.summary: RecoAtlas is designed around exactly the attribution question RQ1 asks: its controlled tool environment exposes agents to semantic, behaviour-aligned or deliberately faulty tools so that performance differences can be diagnosed as coming from stronger reasoning, better signals, or better tool-use policies. Backbones are compared under identical prompts, output schemas, decoding settings, tool budgets and catalog access, and the corruption study keeps prompt, schemas, tool budget and output constraints fixed while degrading only tool quality. The magnitudes are striking for harness attribution: going from zero tools to a full toolset moves bundle SetHit@20 from 0.028 to 0.540, which dwarfs most model-choice effects in the same table, and corrupting the tools halves or quarters performance without touching the model. The authors also caution explicitly that their leaderboard compares complete prompted agents rather than pretrained model quality, because performance depends on how each model interprets the same tool descriptions. Finally, the LLM-judge versus SetHit@20 divergence shows that the choice of evaluator can reverse the ranking a tool change induces.

quotes.text: We compare proprietary and open-weight LLM backbones under identical prompts, output schemas, decoding settings, tool budgets, and catalog access.
The full toolset achieves the best overall utility, reaching 0.508 on comparative shopping and 0.540 on bundle shopping.
At the same time, the leaderboard should be interpreted as a comparison of complete prompted agents, not only of pretrained model quality.

extraction.framework: RecoAtlas
extraction.topology: single-agent tool-using recommendation agent with a budget of 10 tool-decision rounds producing a fixed-size 20-item report
extraction.benchmark: RecoAtlas over three Amazon categories (Musical Instruments, Electronics, Video Games) with 250 queries per category per scenario, yielding 1,500 agent episodes per evaluated method; scored by SetHit@K, learned relevance/complementarity/diversity reward models and LLM judges
extraction.baseline: an in-context LLM with zero tools, plus semantic versus utility-aligned versus faulty tool variants of the same tool interface
extraction.key_results: Tool availability dominates: the zero-tool in-context baseline reaches SetHit@20 of 0.010 comparative and 0.028 bundle; adding search alone gives 0.492 and 0.156; adding substitutability to search preserves comparative but lowers bundle to 0.124; adding complementarity raises bundle to 0.460; the full toolset reaches 0.508 and 0.540. Qwen3 with reasoning enabled scales from about 0.05 at 0.6B to about 0.61 at 32B, while the no-reasoning curve peaks near 14B, giving a roughly 0.31 absolute gap at 32B. Utility degrades monotonically with tool corruption: comparative SetHit@20 falls 0.406 (25% faulty) to 0.205 (75%), bundle 0.392 to 0.124, while diversity rises. LLM-judge scores rank agents with semantic tools above agents with utility-aligned tools despite substantially lower SetHit@20, reversing the ranking induced by downstream utility.
extraction.limitations: The authors note the experiments instantiate the framework on three Amazon categories and fixed evaluation splits; co-purchase labels are treated as behavioural proxies rather than ground truth because they can conflate complementarity with exposure, popularity, bundling or catalog artifacts; RecoAtlas is not a substitute for online experimentation; and the leaderboard is explicitly a comparison of complete prompted agents rather than a pure backbone ranking.

records.title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents

evidence_notes.summary: This synthesis is the closest thing in the batch to a prior statement of RQ1 at review level. Its cross-cutting pattern of uneven returns to additional scaffolding states directly that adding more agents, tools, reasoning effort or context does not uniformly improve reliability and can reduce it, citing multi-agent coordination overhead, context accumulation effects, and the Holistic Agent Leaderboard finding that higher reasoning effort reduced accuracy in most runs. It also documents the reverse direction: TravelPlanner success moves from 0.6% to about 65% when external verifiers and critics are bolted on, which is a harness change producing a hundredfold headline swing with no change to the underlying task. Its measurement-validity cluster supplies the RQ2 framing, arguing that part of the apparent year-over-year improvement in agent scores reflects tightening of evaluation methodology and correction of earlier measurement error rather than capability gain alone. The non-composability pattern (strong single-turn function calling not predicting stateful multi-turn success) further suggests that where a scaffold has to carry state, the scaffold rather than the model is the binding constraint. It contributes no primary measurement and does not itself hold any harness constant.

quotes.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that at least part of the apparent year -over-year improvement in agent benchmark scores reflects tightening of evaluation methodology and correction of earlier measurement error, alongside a genuine rise in underlying capability, rather than one or the other in isolation.
Adding more agents, more tools, more reasoning effort, or more context does not uniformly improve reliability, and can sometimes reduce it.
Agents that correctly execute the large majority of individual tool calls, or that satisfy most individual planning constraints, frequently fail the composed task as a whole.

extraction.topology: n/a (six-cluster taxonomy mapped onto stages of an agent's reasoning-to-action pipeline)
extraction.benchmark: 19 distinct named benchmarks across 27 synthesized papers, including GAIA, WebArena, AgentBench, TravelPlanner, the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard, SWE-bench, ToolEmu, InjecAgent, MAST, METR time horizons and the Holistic Agent Leaderboard
extraction.key_results: Compiled cross-benchmark figures: WebArena rose from about 14% to a reported 61.7% for a specialized enterprise scaffold against about 78% human performance; TravelPlanner moved from 0.6% (GPT-4) to about 10% with reasoning models and about 65% with external formal verifiers and critics; METR reports near-100% success under about four human-minutes and under 10% above about four hours with the 50%-reliability horizon doubling roughly every seven months; SWE-bench success for one configuration fell from about 12.5% to about 4% after leakage correction and stronger generated tests changed leaderboard rankings in about 25-41% of cases; MAST identifies 14 multi-agent failure modes (about 42% specification, 37% inter-agent misalignment, 21% verification); ToolEmu's safest agent still produced severe outcomes in 23.9% of cases; InjecAgent reports about 24% attack success rising to about 47% with a reinforced prompt; models in dedicated function-calling modes produced about 77.5 versus about 21 incorrect function calls on average compared with prompting-based approaches.
extraction.limitations: The authors state this is a narrative rather than a systematic review with no pre-registered protocol, so a different team might draw cluster boundaries differently and some relevant work may be omitted; the field moves quickly and cited figures are frequently superseded; they rely on the source papers' own reported methodology and inter-annotator statistics and did not reproduce any underlying experiment; most cited studies cover English-language text and web tasks; two cited sources are not peer reviewed.

records.title: Perceive, Plan, Act, Self-Correct: An Architectural Framework for Goal-Directed Agentic AI Systems

evidence_notes.summary: Screened core from the abstract, but no full text could be retrieved with the institutional session; recorded as an explicit evidence gap rather than relabelled to let the stopping rule pass.

records.title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation

evidence_notes.summary: HAL is the central RQ1 and RQ2 reference in this batch because it makes scaffold an explicit third evaluation axis alongside model and benchmark, and standardizes the harness so that cross-model comparison is apples-to-apples. Its most consequential RQ2 finding is that prior work almost never did this: only 2 of the nine benchmarks had ever been run with the same scaffold across four or more of the models compared, so most published cross-model agent comparisons confound model with harness by construction. Its RQ1 evidence is direct and large. Scaffold choice alone drives a 9x cost difference for a two-point accuracy difference on the same benchmark, model-scaffold interactions reverse direction by provider (Claude with BrowserUse, OpenAI with SeeAct), and task-specific scaffolds consistently beat a generalist scaffold on the same models and benchmarks. The reasoning-effort result cuts the same way: in 21 of 36 combinations more inference-time compute gave equal or lower accuracy. The log analysis adds a second attribution channel, since agents fail through instruction violations, tool-call failures and environmental barriers in the scaffold or benchmark rather than through reasoning limits, including a leakage bug in an official scaffold that invalidated a completed evaluation.

quotes.text: We found that only 2 of these benchmarks were ever evaluated with the same agent scaffold for 4 or more models from this list, making cross-model comparison hard (Section A9).
Agent scaffolds create drastic differences in cost and accuracy.The choice of scaffold can be consequential in determining the final cost and accuracy of the agent.
In cases where the same models are used for both task-specific and generalist scaffolds across three benchmarks, task-specific agents consistently outperform.

extraction.framework: HAL (Holistic Agent Leaderboard) harness
extraction.topology: task-specific single-agent scaffolds (BrowserUse, SeeAct, Open Deep Research, CORE-Agent, SAB Self-Debug, SciCode Tool Calling, SWE-Agent, USACO Episodic+Semantic) compared against a generalist smolagents scaffold
extraction.benchmark: nine benchmarks across four domains: AssistantBench, CORE-Bench Hard, GAIA, Online Mind2Web, SciCode, ScienceAgentBench, SWE-bench Verified Mini, TAU-bench Airline, USACO
extraction.baseline: the HAL generalist scaffold as a cross-benchmark reference against task-specific scaffolds; low versus high reasoning effort within the same model; cost and token Pareto frontiers including a zero-accuracy zero-cost origin
extraction.key_results: 21,730 agent rollouts across 9 models and 9 benchmarks costing about $40,000 and yielding 2.5B tokens of logs. Higher reasoning effort produced equal or lower accuracy in 21 of 36 model-agent-benchmark combinations. Task-specific scaffolds beat the generalist scaffold on 9 of 12 CORE-Bench Hard runs and 11 of 12 SWE-bench Verified Mini runs, while the generalist was cheaper in 20 of 24 comparisons. On Online Mind2Web, SeeAct with GPT-5 Medium cost $171 against $1,577 for Browser-Use with Claude Sonnet 4, a 9x cost difference for a two-percentage-point accuracy difference; Claude models performed better with BrowserUse and OpenAI models with SeeAct. Only 2 of the nine benchmarks had ever been evaluated with the same agent scaffold for four or more of the listed models in prior work. Log analysis found agents violating an explicit benchmark instruction in over 60% of failed AssistantBench and CORE-Bench tasks, environmental or scaffold barriers in roughly 40% of failed tasks, and a data-leakage bug in the official TAU-bench few-shot scaffold that invalidated those results.
extraction.limitations: The authors state that latency data is confounded by massively parallel evaluation and API rate-limit errors and would be unrepresentative of real-world use; the four domains are not exhaustive and cybersecurity and retail are excluded from this version; automated log analysis covers only three or four of the nine benchmarks; and standardization is hampered because providers swap model weights behind the same endpoint without notice and aggregators can serve different quantizations under the same endpoint name.

records.title: LATS-RCA: Language Agent Tree Search for Root Cause Analysis in Microservices

evidence_notes.summary: This is a rare study that decomposes a multi-agent gain into topology and search-scaffold components rather than reporting a single multi-agent-versus-single-agent delta. Because the two ReAct baselines use the same tools and the same data under the same task formulation, the design separates what specialization plus cross-modal handoff contributes (39.8% to 57.4%) from what the tree-search scaffold adds on top of that same topology (57.4% to 91.3%), and the authors conclude explicitly that multi-agent specialization and handoff alone do not account for the gains. The backbone sweep is the complementary control: with the scaffold fixed, frontier-tier models vary by at most 1.6 percentage points, so within this task the scaffold explains far more of the spread than the model does. The ablation quantifies which harness components carry that scaffold effect (candidate batching 7.0pp, backpropagation 6.5pp, reflection 3.7pp). Cost is reported alongside accuracy, showing that the scaffold buys accuracy with 3.8x tokens and 7.6x runtime rather than with more evidence. The 91.3% to 65.1% benchmark-to-production drop is direct evidence that benchmark-measured scaffold effects overstate deployed performance.

quotes.text: The improvement over the multi-agent ReAct baseline indicates that multi-agent specialization and cross-modal handoff alone do not fully contribute to the gains; rather, the structured search process further strengthens diagnostic accuracy beyond linear cross-modal reasoning under the same tool and data setting.
These results indicate that the diagnostic accuracy gains of LATS-RCA stem from systematic exploration and reflection-guided evaluation, rather than from gathering more monitoring data.
Accuracy varies by at most 1.6 % across frontier-tier models (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro).

extraction.framework: LATS-RCA
extraction.topology: supervisor-worker: a log agent and a metric agent each running reflection-guided Monte Carlo tree search, coordinated by a supervisor with a reflection-triggered handoff and final cross-modal correlation
extraction.benchmark: the public LO2 dataset (lo2-sample: 100 anomaly cases spanning 53 failure types over seven microservices), plus 37 manually labelled real incidents from Zoner Oy's production microservice system
extraction.baseline: two author-constructed ReAct baselines using the same tools and the same log and metric data: a single-agent linear-reasoning baseline and a multi-agent variant executing sequential log-then-metrics analysis
extraction.key_results: On LO2, LATS-RCA reaches 91.3% diagnostic accuracy (standard deviation 1.2% over five runs) against 39.8% for single-agent ReAct and 57.4% for multi-agent ReAct, at 53.1 API calls, 156K tokens and 9.1 minutes versus 13.5/41K/1.2 and 25.2/73K/1.7. It explores 18.9 hypotheses per investigation versus 5.1 and 8.5, a 3.7x increase in search breadth, while all three methods collect about 7.0 evidence items. Ablations: removing candidate batching costs 7.0pp, removing backpropagation 6.5pp, removing reflection 3.7pp. Across frontier-tier backbones accuracy varies by at most 1.6pp (Claude Sonnet 4.5 91.3%, Gemini 3 Pro 90.1%, GPT-5 89.7%), while weaker backbones drop to 79.6% (Claude Haiku 4.5) and 72.8% (GPT-5.2 nano) despite issuing more calls and tokens. In production, accuracy falls to 65.1% on average (range 62-70%) at about 75 calls, 220K tokens and 13 minutes per incident.
