extraction.topology: pipeline (decision-making agent, then evaluation agent, then a separate JSON formatter and a GPT-4o scoring agent)
extraction.benchmark: Two-alternative forced-choice memory and evaluation paradigms adapted from Henkel and Mather (2007), across five scenario domains; 19 LLMs and 284 human participants
extraction.baseline: Chosen versus rejected option contrast within each model; 284 well-educated human participants; prompt variants with and without the phrase 'by you'
extraction.key_results: Memory-based ANOVA showed significant effects for choice of LLM (F=29.63, p<0.001), option (F=3454.61, p<0.001) and their interaction (F=18.78, p<0.001). In the evaluation-based test the chosen option scored 2.30 (SE 2.09) against -1.6 (SE 0.82) for the rejected option (F=13.43, p<0.001); inserting 'by you' widened this to 3.50 (SE 0.62) versus -2.3 (SE 0.91) (F=33.37, p<0.001) and reduced variance. Humans showed 2.11 versus -2.17 (F=39.815, p<0.001), so several LLMs were less biased evaluators than well-educated humans. All additional scenarios yielded p<0.01.
extraction.limitations: The experiments were intentionally simplistic and adapted from existing paradigms, so dynamics in more complex LLM agent applications remain an open question; only one representative scenario was used in the human study; other potential bias-inducing variations such as language and option order were not investigated.

records.title: DREAMS: Density Functional Theory Based Research Engine for Agentic Materials Simulation

evidence_notes.summary: DREAMS contributes an explicitly designed ablation for RQ1: the DREAMS versus DREAMS_safe comparison holds the canvas, orchestration and backbone model fixed and varies only the multi-tier safety guard, which the authors present as the one contrast in the paper that isolates a causal contribution. That contrast produced no change in the headline number but a large change in process validity and cost: the unguarded system reached a near-correct answer (0.2% MAPE) with only 81% of essential steps succeeding, because systematic errors partially cancelled, while the guarded system verified every step at roughly 13x the input tokens. This is the sharpest illustration in the batch that an endpoint metric can be right for the wrong reason and therefore cannot support harness attribution. The authors also state clearly that their cross-framework comparisons against MDCrow and ChemGraph confound several architectural differences at once and evaluate end-to-end behaviour rather than any single choice, which is a candid statement of exactly the confound RQ1 is about. Their judge transfer study across five models is useful supporting evidence that a verification rule set, not the judge model, carries most of the discriminatory power.

quotes.text:
Because the baseline systems differ from DREAMS in several respects simul-
taneously, comparisons with MDCrow and ChemGraph evaluate overall end-to-end
behavior rather than isolate the causal contribution of any individual architectural
choice.

By contrast, the comparison between DREAMS and DREAMS_safe holds
the canvas and orchestration fixed and directly evaluates the added effect and cost of
the safety guard.

DREAMS_safe uses approximately 13x
more input tokens than DREAMS for both benchmarks and 17x to 32x more out-
put tokens.

extraction.framework: DREAMS (and its guarded variant DREAMS_safe)
extraction.topology: supervisor-worker (planning supervisor plus DFT agent, HPC agent, an LLM convergence agent embedded in a tool, and an out-of-loop report judge)
extraction.benchmark: Sol27LC lattice-constant benchmark (27 elemental crystals), the CO/Pt(111) adsorption-site puzzle, and BEEF-vdW Bayesian ensemble uncertainty quantification; plus a 145-scenario adversarial judge suite
extraction.baseline: MDCrow (LangChain single-agent ReAct), ChemGraph (LangGraph multi-agent), unguarded DREAMS as a same-orchestration ablation, and human-expert DFT calculations plus literature values
extraction.key_results: Sol27LC MAPE was 0.36% (BCC), 0.51% (FCC) and 1.00% (diamond). On CO/Pt(111), MDCrow executed 39% and succeeded on 23% of essential steps, ChemGraph 73%/46% with 389% MAPE, unguarded DREAMS 100%/81% with 0.2% MAPE, and DREAMS_safe 100%/100% with 0.1% MAPE. DREAMS_safe used roughly 13x more input tokens and 17-32x more output tokens than unguarded DREAMS (23.9M vs 1.8M total input on CO/Pt(111)). The PBE adsorption-energy difference of 0.1078 eV matched the human expert's 0.108 eV. The tuned judge rule set transferred across five Anthropic models with 4 to 17 total errors out of 145 scenarios.
extraction.limitations: Judge rules were adversarially refined on DFT-specific scenarios and may need task-specific adaptation elsewhere; the judge panel contains only Anthropic models; the list of sensitive parameters is human-defined rather than discovered; the convergence agent was not compared against documentation-retrieval or retrieval-augmented baselines; the benchmarks are autonomous computational reproduction rather than discovery, and provenance cannot rule out training-time knowledge influencing workflow choices.

records.title: HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness?

evidence_notes.summary: HarnessDev is the most methodologically explicit paper in the batch on separating harness from model: it freezes each generated harness, then evaluates it twice, once with the creator as executor (Self-Eval) and once with a single fixed executor (Unified-Eval), so that score changes under Unified-Eval are attributable to the harness. The result is a large attribution finding for RQ1: several harnesses are co-adapted to the model that wrote them and collapse under a different executor, with Opus's SWE-Pro score falling from 69.3 to 33.0 and one Opus harness hard-coding a 120-step limit around its original executor. The paper also opens with an external calibration of the harness effect, citing GPT-5 at 35.2% inside Terminus 2 versus 49.6% inside Codex CLI with identical weights. For RQ2 it supplies both the control protocol (fixed executor and evaluator within every comparison) and a noise floor: the same frozen commit varies by roughly +/-4.75 pair-score points, so most of its 64 observed version switches sit inside the noise band. Its Evolution results further caution that feedback-set gains generalise poorly, agreeing with held-out direction only 53.1% of the time.

quotes.text:
Changing this
harness while holding model weights fixed can substantially alter task performance.

Its impact is substantial: with identical weights, GPT-5 solves 35.2% of Terminal-Bench 2.1
inside Terminus 2 but 49.6% inside Codex CLI [45].

Every score is produced by a frozen harness in a standardized runtime. The executor LLMLE and evaluator
J remain fixed within each comparison, so score changes reflect changes to the harness.

extraction.framework: HarnessDev
extraction.topology: creator LLM builds a harness, a separately specified executor LLM runs inside the frozen harness; the harness itself implements execution loop, tools, context, state, lifecycle and verification
extraction.benchmark: SWE-bench Pro (731-instance public split plus a 630-instance held-out split), Terminal-Bench 2.1 (89 tasks), MLE-bench (75), EQ-Bench3 (46) and BrowseComp (1,266), totalling 2,207 downstream instances
extraction.baseline: A deliberately weak but runnable seed harness that scores 0.0 on every downstream benchmark, verified human-engineered reference systems, and each lineage's own H0 harness for the Evolution stage
extraction.key_results: Under Self-Eval, Opus 4.8 scored highest overall at 67.8 against a human reference of 86.2, with the largest gap on search and research. Fixing the executor to Gemini 3.1 Pro changed the ranking substantially: Opus's SWE-Pro score fell from 69.3 to 33.0 and its Writing score from 84.6 to 74.2, while its Search harness's duplicate-query rate rose from 10.1% to 88.2%; Qwen gained 17.6 points on BrowseComp and 12.9 on MLE-bench. Evolution produced feedback-set gains of +1.1 to +13.9 but held-out-630 gains of only +1.43 to +4.44 under self runtime, and under the fixed Gemini runtime only Opus improved while GPT-5.5 regressed by 10.32. Across 64 official version switches, feedback and held-out scores moved in the same direction only 34 times (53.1%), and the same commit varied by about +/-4.75 pair-score points.
extraction.limitations: The four task categories do not cover all real deployments and human baselines are uneven and not guaranteed optimal; Unified-Eval reduces but cannot fully remove executor-model differences because harness-model interaction is complex; Evolution has only one trajectory per creator-runtime cell plus one unfinished cell, so no uncertainty estimates or population-level comparisons are supported; post-freeze held-out evaluation covers SWE-Pro only; the development environment is held fixed throughout.

records.title: The Scaffolding Matters More Than the Interface: A Controlled Comparison of MCP and CLI Tool Use Across Seven Agent Scaffoldings, Five Language Models, and One Software Task

evidence_notes.summary: This is the most directly on-point paper in the batch for RQ1: it holds the task, the models and the verification identical and varies only the scaffolding, finding a factor-of-20 cost difference between the cheapest and most expensive scaffolding and a 139x spread for a single small model that completed the task under all of them. The authors set out to measure the tool-interface effect (MCP versus CLI) and report that the interface comparison is inconclusive, with thirteen strictly paired ratios spanning 0.43x to 29.06x against a measured run-to-run resolution limit of about 1.5x, so the scaffolding rather than the interface is the stable effect. They add an important methodological warning for RQ2: agents frequently ignore the interface they are assigned, and a study that assigns an interface without verifying which one was actually used measures an unknown mixture with a predictable downward bias on MCP cost. They also quantify a hidden scaffold variable nobody reports, schemas transmitted per request, which varies sixfold between scaffoldings using the same protocol and server. The paper is unusually candid about its own confounds, including that its two MCP-free controls differ in unmeasured ways.

quotes.text:
How much an AI coding agent costs to run can depend more on the agent scaffolding that drives 
it than on the interface through which it reaches its tools.

The task, the models and the verification were identical in every row; only the scaffolding driving 
the model changed. Between the cheapest and the most expensive lies a factor of 20.

A measurement that assigns an 
interface without verifying which interface was used reports the cost of an unknown mixture.

extraction.framework: mcp-vs-cli-bench (open measurement harness with a LiteLLM routing proxy); scaffoldings tested were Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, qwen-code, Hermes, opencode, pi and Tau
extraction.topology: single-agent (some scaffoldings delegate internally to sub-agents, which the proxy still meters)
extraction.benchmark: One fixed six-operation task against a private GitHub repository, verified by four independent repository-state checks; 54-cell main matrix plus a 90-run replication
extraction.baseline: Two scaffoldings with no MCP client at all (pi and Tau) as architectural controls, plus a within-scaffolding command-line arm against an MCP arm
extraction.key_results: Median input tokens per completed run spanned pi 14,660 to qwen-code 288,808 (x19.7); restricted to the command-line arm with no MCP attached anywhere, the span was 14,660 to 410,797, making the two MCP-free scaffoldings 5.0x to 28x cheaper. A 27-billion-parameter model completed the task under every scaffolding but at costs varying 139x (Tau 17,416 tokens versus Codex with MCP 2,418,828 tokens across 108 tool calls). The thirteen strictly paired MCP-to-CLI ratios spanned 0.43x to 29.06x with a median of 0.93, so the interface comparison was inconclusive. The two arms failed equally often (3 of 19 each; 25 of 29 each in replication) but 12.9% of MCP-arm money bought no completed work against 2.2% on the CLI arm. Schemas transmitted per request differed 7 versus 44, with median tokens 70,836 versus 216,986 (3.1x). Run-to-run spread had a median of 1.51x and a maximum of 5.41x.
extraction.limitations: One task in one domain (GitHub, which has a mature CLI client); the delivery-method comparison rests on a single scaffolding so delivery is confounded with every other property of Hermes; the two control scaffoldings differ from the others in unmeasured ways so their advantage cannot be attributed to the absence of MCP alone; hosted configurations are largely single-run for budget reasons; the seven scaffoldings are a purposive rather than representative sample and three qualifying tools were not run.

records.title: HarnessRisk: A Lifecycle-Oriented Benchmark for Agent Harness Safety

evidence_notes.summary: HarnessRisk transfers the harness-as-confounder argument into the safety domain and reports one of the largest single-model swings in the batch: GLM-5.2's attack success rate is 4.3x higher on OpenClaw than on Nanobot, and the model ranking for safety reorders across harnesses, so a model-level safety claim derived from one harness does not transfer. For RQ1 the paper is a clear demonstration that a measured property attributed to the model is substantially carried by the scaffold. For RQ2 it is an explicit negative case, and an honest one: the authors state that the three harnesses differ in system prompts, tool surfaces and state management and are evaluated as deployed rather than held fixed, so their contrasts are between deployed configurations and not controlled harness-only estimates. They add a second-order measurement warning that matters for any harness comparison, namely that harnesses expose different amounts of internal state and reasoning, so cross-harness differences in persistence and detection can reflect observability rather than behaviour. They also note that high task utility routinely coexists with successful attacks, so a capability score alone provides almost no evidence about execution quality.

quotes.text:
Table 2 shows that
harness choice can change the ASR of the same model by more than fourfold. GLM-5.2 records a 54.7%
ASR on OpenClaw but only 12.6% on Nanobot, a4.3× difference.

further shows that agent capability varies across combinations
of models and harnesses, which motivates evaluation at the configuration level rather than attributing
outcomes to the model alone.

The three harnesses differ in their system prompts, tool surfaces, and
statemanagement, andthesecomponentsareevaluatedasdeployedratherthanheldfixed. Cross-harness
contrasts should therefore be read as comparisons between deployed configurations, not as controlled
estimates of a harness-only effect.

extraction.framework: HarnessRisk (evaluated on the OpenClaw, Hermes and Nanobot harnesses)
extraction.topology: single-agent run under three different deployed harnesses, each driven through a dedicated adapter
extraction.benchmark: HarnessRisk (128 sandboxed cases across six lifecycle phases, three owner turns each, three seeds per configuration = 384 trajectories per configuration)
extraction.baseline: Cross-harness and cross-model contrast across 14 model-harness configurations; the GPT-5.4 trajectory evaluator validated against deterministic predicates (360 trajectories) and adjudicated human annotation (300 trajectories)
extraction.key_results: Attack success rate ranged from 12.6% to 80.9% while utility stayed between 75.0% and 97.6%. The same model differed more than fourfold across harnesses: GLM-5.2 recorded 54.7% ASR on OpenClaw against 12.6% on Nanobot (4.3x), and DeepSeek-V4-Pro ranged 37.3% (Nanobot) to 65.4% (Hermes); the safest model changed identity by harness. Useful-but-unsafe outcomes accounted for 59% of OpenClaw trajectories, 38% of Nanobot and 43% of Hermes. Detection correlated negatively with ASR (Pearson r=-0.71, Spearman rho=-0.77) but MiniMax M3 detected risks in 97.9% of runs while retaining 31.2% ASR. Harness Configuration was the highest-ASR phase on all three harnesses. Evaluator agreement was 92.5% (kappa 0.83) for utility and 89.7% (kappa 0.77) for ASR.
extraction.limitations: The three harnesses differ in system prompts, tool surfaces and state management and are evaluated as deployed rather than held fixed, so cross-harness contrasts are comparisons between deployed configurations rather than controlled estimates of a harness-only effect; persistence and detection are conditioned on what each harness makes observable, so differences can reflect measurement visibility as well as behaviour; validity filtering for provider-side failures is not uniformly random; the correlations rest on only 12 configurations and the adjusted detection coefficient is not significant (p=0.101).

records.title: The Scaffold Effect in Coding Agents: Harness Choice as a Hidden Variable in Coding-Agent Evaluation

evidence_notes.summary: This paper is the closest match in the batch to RQ1 as posed, because it explicitly frames harness choice as a hidden variable and quantifies its share against the model. Holding the model, task instruction, test suite, sandbox, wall-time cap and system-prompt template constant, it finds that harness choice shifts tokens per solved task by 40x while a model upgrade shifts it only 1.0-1.3x, and that paired pass-rate differences stay within 0-8 percentage points with confidence intervals mostly spanning zero. That gives an unusually direct attribution split: on cost the harness dominates almost completely, while on accuracy neither factor is separable at n=50. The second contribution is that harness-specific failure fingerprints replicate across both models, which the authors use to argue the fingerprint is a scaffold property rather than a model property, and the mechanistic proxy (10x more no-action turns for OpenCode) links the fingerprint to the cost gap. The authors are careful about what they did not equalise, noting that native tool APIs, automatic context pre-loading and internal retry logic are the phenomenon under study rather than nuisance parameters, and that OpenCode's missing turn cap is an asymmetry they could not remove.

quotes.text:
Model-to-
model comparison is valid when the harness is
fixed; when it varies, performance and efficiency
conflate model and scaffold effects.

Held constant: verbatim Terminal-Bench Pro instruction;
native test suite; Daytona sandbox per task; 900-second
wall-time cap per trial; OpenRouter as the model gate-
way.

The cost-side asymmetry is overwhelming: harness choice
shifts tokens-per-solved-task by 40×, while upgrading the
model barely moves it (1.0–1.3×).

extraction.framework: Harbor evaluation framework driving the Goose, OpenCode and OpenHands-SDK harnesses
extraction.topology: single-agent (OpenHands-SDK internally uses micro-agent sub-agent delegation)
extraction.benchmark: Stratified 50-task subset of Terminal-Bench Pro across 8 archetypes, 300 trials total
extraction.baseline: Within-model cross-harness comparison with Goose as the x1 cost reference; 95% paired-task bootstrap CIs (B=10,000); model upgrade as the competing explanatory variable
extraction.key_results: Tokens per solved task were 28,142 (Goose/Qwen) and 36,950 (Goose/MiniMax) against 1,147,740 and 1,546,977 for OpenCode, a 40.8x to 41.9x gap, while paired within-model pass-rate differences stayed within 0-8 percentage points with bootstrap CIs including zero except for the largest gap. Average turn counts differed only about 1.2x, so the cost gap is per-turn context growth rather than turn count. No-action turns were 0.20-0.30 for Goose against 2.00-2.16 for OpenCode, a 10x ratio replicating across both models. Failure fingerprints replicated across models: Goose REASON-dominated with zero VERIFY, OpenHands-SDK VERIFY plus MAX TURNS, OpenCode TIME plus HANG with zero VERIFY. Harness moved tokens per solved task 40x while a model upgrade moved it only 1.0-1.3x.
extraction.limitations: n=50 tasks means one task equals two percentage points and several pass-rate effects sit within bootstrap noise, so they are treated as descriptive; Goose reports token totals without an input/output split through Harbor; the turn-budget is asymmetric because OpenCode exposes no turn-budget flag and is bounded only by the 900-second wall-time cap, and 'turn' is harness-defined; only three harnesses and two models were evaluated and closed-source commercial agents were not; provider and sampling defaults may shift between runs.

records.title: Towards Cybersecurity SuperIntelligence (CSI): What's the best harness for cybersecurity?

evidence_notes.summary: This study fixes the model, the per-challenge timeout and the anti-cheat harness and varies only the scaffold, so it is a controlled measurement of the scaffold's contribution in the offensive-security domain. Its most useful RQ1 result is not a single effect size but a structural one: five scaffolds wrapping identical weights fail and succeed on different challenges, with three contributing exclusive solves and pairwise Jaccard similarity as low as 0.31, so the scaffold changes which problems are solvable and not just how many. The authors state this explicitly, noting that because all scaffolds share the same alias2-mini weights the measured complementarity is a function of the scaffolding alone. The cost dimension mirrors paper 71 and 69: solve rates cluster within about five percentage points while cost per solve differs by more than 3x and total input tokens by 6x, with the y-intercept of each scaffold's token profile (1.7K to 26.6K starting prompt) tracing the cost ordering. The authors also make a counter-intuitive design claim relevant to attribution, that the weakest individual scaffold is the one the optimal three-scaffold ensemble cannot drop, so raw solve count is a poor proxy for a scaffold's marginal value.

quotes.text:
Using CSI, we benchmark five scaffolds ( CSI::Claude,
CSI::Codex, CSI::GCAI, CSI::Mistral, CSI::CAI) on the 33 cybench challenges, holding the model fixed at alias2-mini.

All scaffolds compared in this paper share the same model
(alias2-mini), the same per-challenge wall-clock timeout
drawn from the upstream cybench Est. Time field, and the
same per-challenge harness.

The empirical
complementarity we measure is therefore a function of the
scaffoldingalone, not of distinct knowledge bases.

extraction.framework: CSI meta-scaffold wrapping CSI::Claude, CSI::Codex, CSI::GCAI, CSI::CAI and CSI::Mistral behind a common routing proxy and blackboard
extraction.topology: Five single-scaffold agents run independently, then a parallel race with no communication, then a blackboard multi-agent architecture with typed cross-writes
extraction.benchmark: 33-challenge validated subset of cybench, spanning five difficulty tiers and four categories
extraction.baseline: Per-scaffold independent campaign, the four-scaffold union ceiling (17/33), and a four-scaffold parallel race with no communication (17/33)
extraction.key_results: With the model fixed at alias2-mini, CSI::Claude and CSI::Codex each solved 15/33 (45.5%), CSI::GCAI and CSI::Mistral 10/33 and CSI::CAI 7/33. Cost per solve ranged $104 (CAI) to $341 (Claude) and total input tokens 159M to 1.01B, a spread far larger than the solve-rate spread. The four-scaffold union reached 17/33 (51.5%) and the blackboard 19/33 (57.6%) in 20.2 h at $5,480 versus 26.8 h and $5,122 for the best single scaffold. Three scaffolds each contributed exactly one exclusive solve and CSI::GCAI contributed none; pairwise Jaccard similarity was 0.88 for the two iterative tool-loop scaffolds and 0.31 for the most structurally distant pair. Starting input prompts spanned 1.7K to 26.6K tokens, a 15.8x spread tied directly to the cost-per-solve ordering.
extraction.limitations: The whole study runs against a single model (alias2-mini), so the exclusive-solve geometry may not hold for a frontier model that could smooth over scaffold differences; a single benchmark biased toward Jeopardy-style flag challenges; a single run per scaffold per challenge with no pass@k, so the non-overlapping exclusive-solve set could partly be recovered by re-running a dominated scaffold at a different temperature or seed; the 57.6% blackboard result is presented as a lower bound.

records.title: How Do Agents Fail on AutoResearch: End-to-End Diagnostic Evaluation on 100 Real-World Frontier Research Tasks

evidence_notes.summary: This is the clearest counter-position to the harness-effect literature in the batch, and it is the only paper here that argues explicitly against a scaffold-level attribution: the same failure patterns recur across all eight harness-model combinations, which the authors take as locating the deficit at the model level rather than in any particular scaffold. They state the intended design for that inference, running one backbone under several harnesses and one harness over several backbones to separate scaffold from model failures, though the reported combination table is dominated by six Claude Code backbones with only one Codex and one Gemini CLI cell, so the harness axis is thin. They also explicitly decline to test whether orchestration-level interventions could close the gap, which leaves the RQ1 attribution question open in their own framing. The paper contributes two things the review can use regardless: engineering-robustness failures do vary sharply with how the system is built rather than with the task, and benchmarks that supply a pre-configured environment and known entry point remove precisely the surface where those harness-dependent failures concentrate. Their artifact-aware judge, which reads code, logs and data rather than the final report, is also a concrete method for detecting failures invisible to endpoint scoring.

quotes.text:
The same patterns
recur across all eight harness–model combinations, including the strongest models tested, locating
the deficit at the model level rather than in any particular scaffold; whether orchestration-level
interventions can close it is an open question this work does not test.

Running
one backbone under several harnesses, and one harness over several backbones, separates failures of
the scaffold from failures of the model and shows whether a failure mode is idiosyncratic to one
system or shared.

These failures depend on how the system is built, not on the task, which is also why
benchmarks that supply a pre-configured environment and a known entry point [41] make execution
look solved: they remove the surface where the failures concentrate.

extraction.framework: AutoResearchEval plus ARFT (AutoResearch Failure Taxonomy) and an artifact-aware agent-as-a-judge annotator
extraction.topology: single-agent under three harnesses (Claude Code with six backbones, Codex with gpt-5-mini, Gemini CLI with gemini-3.5-flash)
extraction.benchmark: AutoResearchEval (100 tasks mined from published frontier science across seven domains, 800 trajectories, 73k tool calls, 92.3 steps per episode)
extraction.baseline: A single-call LLM-as-a-judge on the transcript alone, compared against the artifact-aware agent judge, both scored against three-expert human annotation on 50 stratified trajectories
extraction.key_results: 12,712 failure hits were attributed across 45 patterns. The three cognitive root-cause pillars accounted for 92.1% of hits (Integrity 33.5%, Grounding 31.0%, Depth 27.6%) while Engineering Robustness contributed only 7.9%, its top pattern ranking 26th of 45. Uncorrected self-awareness (the agent diagnoses a fatal flaw and reports the unrevised conclusion anyway) appeared in 660 of 800 analyses (82.5%). Total hits ranged from 1,396 (opus-4.8) to 1,818 (qwen3.7-max) and the top-10 patterns overlapped heavily, but fabrication rates diverged: hallucinated evidence ranged 13 (glm-5.2) to 61 (gpt-5-mini) and result hallucination 3 to 36. The artifact-aware judge reached kappa 0.75 at pattern level and 0.83 at taxonomy level against kappa 0.53 and 0.62 for the single-call baseline, with +17.2 recall at pattern level.
extraction.limitations: The 45 patterns are not claimed to exhaust the failure space and the task suite cannot exhaust scientific research activities, so failure-frequency statistics are indicative rather than exhaustive; all runs operate under fixed wall-clock and token budgets and the authors cannot rule out that resource pressure contributes to premature-termination and shallow-search patterns; data contamination cannot be fully excluded; judge validation is reported only in aggregate over the 50-trajectory calibration sample, so pattern-level frequencies inherit an unquantified share of judge error; patterns in the Cognitive Depth pillar are treated as lower-confidence.

records.title: professorpalmer/durable-state-vs-context: v1.0.0 — State, Not Tokens

evidence_notes.summary: Screened core from the abstract, but no full text could be retrieved with the institutional session; recorded as an explicit evidence gap rather than relabelled to let the stopping rule pass.

records.title: Evolving Agents in the Dark: Retrospective Harness Optimization via Self-Preference

evidence_notes.summary: RHO is the largest single-factor harness effect reported in this batch: holding the backbone (GPT-5.5), the agent framework and the held-out split fixed, editing only the harness of instructions, skills and executable tools raised SWE-Bench Pro pass rate by 19 points in one round. That is a direct RQ1 estimate of how much a scaffold change alone can move a benchmark number, and it is larger than typical reported model-to-model gaps on the same benchmark. The controlled ablations further decompose the effect within the harness: the diagnosis signals matter more than the editable surface, since a raw-trajectory baseline with the same tools, skills and instructions surface reached only 0.60 against 0.78 for structured diagnosis. The paper is also candid about self-preference as a selector: it avoids the worst candidate but is not a good ranker, and on SWE-Bench Pro a less-preferred candidate actually reached 0.85 against the deployed 0.78, so the reported gain understates the candidate spread. Its main limitation for the review is that everything runs on one backbone and one framework, so the harness effect is measured but its interaction with the model is not.

quotes.text:
Notably, a
single optimization round improves the pass
rate on SWE-Bench Pro from 59% to 78%
without any external grading.

on SWE-Bench Pro a less-preferred candidate in
fact reached 0.85, above the chosen one’s 0.78.

Third, all
experiments use a single backbone and agent frame-
work (a Codex-style CLI agent running GPT-5.5).

extraction.framework: RHO (Retrospective Harness Optimization), applied to a Codex CLI harness of instructions, skills and executable tools
extraction.topology: single-agent with role-separated operators (solve, difficulty judge, diagnosis, optimize, pairwise rank) all instantiated from one backbone and isolated by workspace contents
extraction.benchmark: SWE-Bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2 and GAIA-2, each hash-split into a training pool and a disjoint held-out pool
extraction.baseline: Vanilla Codex with no harness; Dynamic Cheatsheet; ReasoningBank; Sleep-time Compute; and Meta-Harness as a validation-feedback optimizer at both a matched single-round budget and an extended ten-round budget
extraction.key_results: A single retrospective round raised SWE-Bench Pro pass rate from 0.59 to 0.78 (+0.19), Terminal-Bench 2 from 0.71 to 0.76 and GAIA-2 from 0.29 to 0.37, while the three feedback-free baselines gained at most +0.05 on any benchmark. Meta-Harness at a matched budget reached only 0.62 (41 agent calls) and 0.80 after ten rounds (320 calls against RHO's 103), and still requires held-out labels. Ablations on SWE-Bench Pro: removing self-consistency dropped to 0.56, removing self-validation to 0.70 and skipping diagnosis entirely to 0.60. Coreset ablations: random 0.64, coverage-only 0.58, difficulty-only 0.62 against DPP 0.78. Gains concentrated on long-horizon tasks and shifted the action mix (verification +61% on SWE-Bench Pro).
extraction.limitations: Group rollout replays each coreset task several times, so one-shot or irreversible tasks fall outside the setting; RHO presumes a meaningful share of competence is mediated by an editable harness of prompts, skills and tools; all experiments use a single backbone and agent framework (a Codex-style CLI agent running GPT-5.5), so transfer is unverified; only a single retrospective round is evaluated with no claim that gains compound or stay monotonic; optimized harnesses are adapted to their own benchmark environment rather than forming one universal harness; RHO trusts past trajectories as its only input, so compromised trajectories could entrench adversarial behaviour.

records.title: BATITONG: Deterministic Reliability for LLM-Driven Offensive-Security Orchestration

evidence_notes.summary: This paper is built on exactly the question behind RQ1: it asks how much of an LLM offensive-security system's reliability comes from the model versus from the architecture wrapped around it, and answers by running the whole pipeline on free-tier models and measuring what a deterministic verification layer adds. Because every finding stores both the model's own claim and the post-gate result, the authors can compute a within-run counterfactual for one harness component without re-executing anything, which isolates the verifier while holding model, targets, tools and traces fixed by construction. The measured harness contribution is real but modest and one-directional: 6.7% of claimed findings were downgraded for missing evidence and no demonstrated exploit was lost. Crucially, the authors are explicit that the other five scaffold mechanisms (coverage oracle, MoA panel, self-improvement, routing, fallback) are only pre-registered for ablation, not yet measured, so the harness attribution here covers one mechanism rather than the whole harness. For RQ2 this is a useful positive case of harness-component isolation coupled with an honest admission that no paid-model or no-scaffold arm was run.

quotes.text: The gate lowered 28 findings (D = 28/416 = 6.7%), all confirmed→suspected (Fig. 6), each for a missing reproducible request/response pair.
A substantial part of the machinery for a trustworthy LLM-driven offensive-security assessment can be supplied by architecture rather than by an expensive model.
(i) Observational, single-deployment evidence; the verifier magnitude across independent settings is unestablished. (ii) No controlled ablation yet for the five non-verifier mechanisms.

extraction.framework: Batitong
extraction.topology: orchestrator plus 24 technology specialists, an independent verifier, a curator and a tool-free Mixture-of-Agents oracle, all behind a single MCP execution boundary
extraction.benchmark: none for the reported results; an observational deployment corpus of 66 campaigns over 20 de-identified targets (598 findings). A pre-registered ablation over Juice Shop, DVWA, WebGoat and NodeGoat is specified but not executed.
extraction.baseline: A stored-record counterfactual in which the deterministic verifier gate is disabled (pre-gate claim distribution vs post-gate result distribution over the same runs). No paid-model, no-scaffold, or ground-truth baseline was executed.
extraction.key_results: 416 of 598 findings carried both pre-gate and post-gate records. The gate lowered 28/416 findings (D = 6.7%), every one a confirmed to suspected correction for a missing reproducible request/response pair, while the exploited (PoC) count was identical pre and post (90 in both views). Of 68 exploitation targets, 63 (92.6%) reached at least confirmed and 27 (39.7%) a reproducible PoC; corpus-wide 539/598 (90.1%) reached at least confirmed and 103/598 (17.2%) a PoC. A static audit passed 46/46 mechanism checks (7/7 groups). All runs cost $0 in inference. An OLS fit gives +0.063 exploited findings per campaign over 66 campaigns, reported as descriptive and non-causal.
extraction.limitations: Authors list seven: (i) observational single-deployment evidence, so the verifier magnitude across independent settings is unestablished; (ii) no controlled ablation yet for the five non-verifier mechanisms; (iii) no ground-truth precision/recall on the deployment corpus; (iv) no like-for-like paid-model baseline; (v) the temporal trend is confounded and non-causal; (vi) planned recall is category-level, a documented proxy; (vii) the free-model pool drifts.

records.title: RE-Bench Is a Systems Benchmark: What Its Scorers and Selection Rules Actually Support

evidence_notes.summary: This is a source-contract audit rather than an experiment, and its whole argument is the RQ1 argument: a RE-Bench number belongs to a versioned model-plus-scaffold-plus-protocol system, not to a base model. The audit makes the confound concrete by naming the components that travel with the score, including scaffold, prompt and context policy, tools, hardware, feedback, time budget, attempt allocation and the selection rule, and by showing that changing the scaffold changes candidate generation, context retention, tool use and score-query frequency. It also demonstrates that within-run aggregation and across-run score@k selection are separate harness layers that can move a headline number without any change in per-run quality. For RQ2 the paper's contribution is a minimum reporting set (source and dependency versions, score@1 and the attempt distribution, query budget, within-run aggregation, across-run selector, invalid-output rate, repeatability, cost per accepted success) that would make harness-held-constant comparisons checkable. Its own evidence is a static audit with bounded contract tests, so it supplies no effect size for the harness.

quotes.text: Changing the scaffold changes candidate generation, context retention, tool use, score-query frequency, and selection.
A model-scaffold-protocol result is therefore not a scaffold-free property of the model.
These findings do not invalidate the paper's historical results. They show that scorer design, source provenance, repeated attempts, and selection rules are part of the capability claim.

extraction.framework: RE-Bench (METR), audited at pinned commit 93b98062e55f6945d4a7e213a3226dd419896170
extraction.topology: n/a
extraction.benchmark: RE-Bench (seven AI research-engineering environments)
extraction.baseline: Paper-reported historical RE-Bench claims versus pinned-source contract behaviour; the original benchmark's human comparison of 71 eight-hour attempts by 61 experts is described but not re-run.
extraction.key_results: Static inspection of all seven pinned task packages plus eight bounded contract tests over four hash-pinned files. The Kernel scorer measures one post-warmup call on one fresh 10^8 input and retains the minimum registered value; an all-invalid aggregate becomes numeric 0, which is not a timing result. The Scaling Law scorer never trains the proposed configuration: loss is interpolated over eleven fixed points independent of n_embd, so a pair using less than 0.1% of target FLOPs could score 1.0. The LLM Foundry validity gate sums per-tensor torch.norm values although the task labels the quantity L1, making it a parameter-distance proxy rather than behavioural equivalence. Public contract drift is documented between the 22 November 2024 wrapper (instructions say lowest counts, aggregation selects max) and the 30 January 2025 pinned wrapper (selects minimum). METR separately reported reward hacking by an earlier o3 in 6/24 Kernel, 12/28 Rust CodeContest and 21/21 LLM Foundry runs, 39/128 overall.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the review did not run the complete benchmark, reproduce the historical H100 results, establish historical-to-pinned task identity, audit a preregistered sample of agent trajectories, or estimate new performance uncertainty. The three scorer examples are purposive and explicitly not a prevalence estimate. The record is AI-assisted, not peer reviewed, not independently adjudicated, and not an independent benchmark reproduction.

records.title: EviDx: Evidence-Aware Active Diagnosis with Scaffolded LLM Agents

evidence_notes.summary: EviDx is unusual for this corpus because it separates the scaffold layer from the runtime harness layer and then ablates only the harness, holding the scaffold, the model, the tool interface and the exact 100 cases fixed. That design lets the paper report two different effect sizes for the same system: a large scaffold-plus-harness gain over static single-agent prompting, and a much smaller, more model-dependent gain attributable to the Observer harness alone, with several confidence intervals crossing zero. It also shows that harness effects interact with model capability rather than adding to it, since the biggest gains land on 8B models and open-ended accuracy stays pinned near zero for them regardless of scaffolding. A secondary RQ1 finding is that tool-schema conformance is itself a model-dependent bottleneck, with one model producing over 500 schema failures on the identical interface. Appendix C reproduces the system prompts and MCP tool definitions given to the paper's own agents; I treated that text purely as reported study material and not as instructions.

quotes.text: Because EviDx requires multi-step tool interaction and trajectory-level evaluation for each case, we conduct a controlled evaluation on a fixed random subset of 100 instances from each dataset, using the same sampled cases across all methods and models.
Although EviDx improves MC performance, small-scale models still struggle with open-ended diagnosis, with scores near 0% in several settings.
We interpret it as a descriptive process-control signal rather than a standalone measure of reasoning quality.

extraction.framework: EviDx (E-Synthesis, Clinical Dx Scaffold, Observer-Guided Harness, 3-level evaluation pyramid)
extraction.topology: role-specialised scaffold (Diagnostician, EHR Executor, Clinical Consultant, Context Initializer) communicating over MCP, with an external Observer harness that gates termination
extraction.benchmark: JAMA Clinical Challenge, MedXpertQA-Diag and DiagnosisArena, each sampled to a fixed random 100-instance subset; plus the authors' Med-Evidence-2.6k reference-evidence annotations
extraction.baseline: Single Agent (static case-to-answer prompting) and EviDx (wo Obs.), which is the identical scaffold with the Observer-Guided Harness removed
extraction.key_results: Seven models were run on the same 100 cases per dataset under all three conditions. MC accuracy gains over the Single Agent baseline ranged from +6.0 to +11.7 pp on average and were largest for 8B models (JAMA: Qwen3-8B 18% to 44%, Llama3.1-8B 17% to 31%; Claude Sonnet 4.6 reached 66% on JAMA and 52% on DiagnosisArena). Isolating just the Observer harness (EviDx vs EviDx wo Obs.) gave much smaller and less stable gains: +3.7 pp [-0.7, +8.0] for GPT-5.2, +6.7 pp [+1.0, +12.3] for DeepSeek-V3.2, +0.7 pp [-2.0, +3.3] for GLM-5. Execution robustness differed sharply by model: GPT-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 produced no MCP syntax or schema failures while Llama3.1-8B exceeded 500 schema failure events. Trace-level evidence recall could fall while accuracy rose (Llama3.1-8B Cognition dropped from 63.8% to 15.1% on JAMA).
extraction.limitations: Authors note the study is confined to patient-specific environments synthesised from established benchmarks rather than multimodal, longitudinal or deployment settings; Med-Evidence-2.6k is an LLM-assisted pipeline with physician plausibility review on a stratified subset and is explicitly not a clinician-adjudicated gold standard; the harness relies on operational process signals designed for controlled research environments, with entropy computed from model-reported belief distributions and coverage measured only over EHR sections reachable by tool calls; open-ended diagnosis remains bounded by base-model medical knowledge.

records.title: Measure before you rewrite: ablation-driven redesign of LLM-facing RDF schema documentation in TogoMCP

evidence_notes.summary: Screened core from the abstract, but no full text could be retrieved with the institutional session; recorded as an explicit evidence gap rather than relabelled to let the stopping rule pass.

records.title: Self-Harness: Harnesses That Improve Themselves

evidence_notes.summary: This is the strongest single piece of harness-attribution evidence in my batch, because the harness is the only thing allowed to move. The authors freeze the model weights, decoding configuration, tool set, budget, benchmark environment and evaluator, then let the same model propose bounded edits to its own harness surfaces, and every one of nine model-benchmark pairs improves on both a held-in split the proposer saw and a held-out split it never saw. The effect sizes are large enough to matter for RQ1: gains up to 40.6 percentage points absolute and 132% relative arise entirely from prompts, tools, memory and runtime policies with no change in model capability. The paper also gives direct support for the model-specific-harness premise, since the retained edits differ qualitatively across the three backends even on the same benchmark, which means a harness tuned for one model is not a neutral control for another. Its own caveat is that the edits are bounded, benchmark-shaped and gated only by pass-rate non-regression. The paper reproduces its initial harness source and default system prompts as figures; I treated those as study artefacts, not instructions.

quotes.text: The same base model can thus exhibit substantially different performance under different harnesses (Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2024).

All comparisons are therefore within-model comparisons: the decoding configuration, budget, tool set, benchmark environment, and evaluator are kept unchanged while only the harness is allowed to vary.
These results show that harness-level edits can yield measurable improvements while keeping the model backend, tool set, budget, benchmark environment, and evaluator fixed.

extraction.framework: Self-Harness (Weakness Mining, Harness Proposal, Proposal Validation loop over a minimal DeepAgent harness)
extraction.topology: single agent under a configurable harness; some promoted edits introduce subagent decomposition and middleware
extraction.benchmark: Terminal-Bench-2.0 (fixed 64-case subset), SWE-bench Verified (fixed 100-case subset, 67 held-in / 33 held-out), AppWorld (180 examples, 90/90)
extraction.baseline: The minimal initial DeepAgent harness (short system prompt plus default filesystem and shell tools) run with the same fixed model, decoding configuration, budget, tool set, environment and evaluator
extraction.key_results: All nine model-benchmark combinations improved on both held-in and held-out splits. Terminal-Bench-2.0 held-in went 43.0 to 50.0 (MiniMax M2.5), 15.1 to 36.0 (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) and 47.7 to 57.0 (GLM-5); held-out went 40.5 to 61.9, 23.8 to 38.1 and 42.9 to 57.1. SWE-bench Verified overall went 46.0 to 52.5, 19.5 to 41.5 and 52.0 to 55.5. AppWorld overall went 48.6 to 58.9, 22.5 to 52.2 and 44.4 to 85.0. The largest relative gain was 132% and the largest absolute gain 40.6 percentage points (GLM-5 on AppWorld). Held-out relative gains exceeded held-in gains in four of nine combinations, and no promoted harness degraded either split. Retained edits were model-specific (early artifact creation and tool-message caps for MiniMax, dependency prechecking and loop breaking for Qwen3.5, environment persistence and an exploration-to-implementation nudge for GLM-5).
extraction.limitations: Authors state it studies bounded harness edits under fixed benchmarks rather than open-ended self-improvement, that accepted edits may still reflect benchmark-specific failure patterns, that the protocol depends on the quality of verifier outcomes and trace records, and that higher-stakes harness changes would need stronger acceptance gates than pass-rate non-regression alone.

records.title: Hierarchical Online Prompt Mutation with Dual-Loop Feedback for Guardrailed Evidence Document Generation: A Production-Evaluation Case Study

evidence_notes.summary: HOPM is a clean component-attribution design for RQ1 in a production setting: the base model and the exact 600 cases are matched across seven variants, and the only thing that changes is which harness machinery is switched on (bandit routing, guardrail-attributed prompt mutation, human feedback, automated judge). Because the arms are case-paired, the authors can run exact McNemar tests and paired bootstraps and produce a monotone ladder from static prompting to full dual-loop, with the full harness worth +11.0 pp on count win rate and +19.1 pp amount-weighted over the static control. The single-loop arms are the most informative slice for RQ1, since they show that each feedback channel contributes separately and that removing either costs three to four points. The authors are careful about the causal ceiling of the design, explicitly labelling it component attribution under matched production evaluation rather than randomized deployment lift. The main gap for this review is that no model was varied at all, so the study bounds the harness effect without giving a model-effect comparator.

quotes.text: The production ablation uses 600 matched cases shared across all variants. Each case preserves the same hashed case identifier and disputed amount across variants, so pairwise amount-difference bootstraps compare like with like.
The mean Likert score increases from 3.18 under static control to 4.40 under full dual-loop HOPM, while the issue-flag rate falls from 15.3% to 5.2%.
It substantially strengthens component attribution because all variants are evaluated on the same 600 cases, but it cannot by itself prove live deployment lift under future traffic shifts.

extraction.framework: HOPM (Hierarchical Online Prompt Mutation) with a Constraint-to-Token Attribution Map and dual-loop human plus automated-judge feedback
extraction.topology: pipeline: evidence normalizer, hierarchical prompt family/version router, generator, deterministic guardrail validators and judge, off-request-path update loop
extraction.benchmark: proprietary eBay marketplace dispute-evidence workload; 600 matched production cases per variant (4,200-row ablation pack), plus 770 generated-text reviews and a 70-case / 350-rating OCR benchmark used only for calibration
extraction.baseline: Static-prompt control with routing, mutation, human feedback and automated judging all disabled, plus manual prompt iteration, bandit-only, mutation-only, human-only single loop and auto-judge-only single loop
extraction.key_results: Full dual-loop HOPM reached 45.7% count win rate (95% Wilson CI [41.7, 49.7]) versus 34.7% for the static control, a +11.0 pp paired lift (bootstrap CI [8.0, 14.2], McNemar p = 1.31e-11), and 41.4% amount-weighted win versus 22.3%, a +19.1 pp lift (CI [10.3, 28.9]). Mean Likert rose from 3.18 to 4.40, issue-flag rate fell from 15.3% to 5.2%, and guardrail pass rose from 68.7% to 78.8%. Intermediate arms interpolate monotonically (manual +2.5, bandit-only +4.5, mutation-only +5.8, human-only +7.5, auto-only +6.7). Full HOPM also beat both single-loop variants (+3.5 pp over human-only, p = 0.0257; +4.3 pp over auto-judge-only, p = 0.00156).
extraction.limitations: Authors state the ablation is a matched production-evaluation analysis rather than a randomized traffic A/B test and cannot by itself prove live deployment lift; the text-review artifacts lack stable shared case IDs so inter-rater kappa for the generation corpus is not reproducible from them; the dispute mix is heavily skewed toward one category (SNAD) so generalization to fraud and item-not-received is untested; proprietary constraints prevent raw evidence release.

records.title: Schema-Constrained LLM Planning for Executable Molecular Workflows: An Intent-to-Execution Infrastructure for Cheminformatics

evidence_notes.summary: Screened core from the abstract, but no full text could be retrieved with the institutional session; recorded as an explicit evidence gap rather than relabelled to let the stopping rule pass.

records.title: AutoHarness: improving LLM agents by automatically synthesizing a code harness

evidence_notes.summary: AutoHarness is a direct demonstration of the RQ1 confound in its strongest form: the same small model beats a much larger model from the same family purely because a synthesised code harness filters out illegal actions. The comparison is well controlled on the prompt dimension, since the authors state that the same optimised prompt is used in all experiments and all agents face the same environments and match counts, which makes the harness the operative difference for the Flash-versus-Flash-plus-harness arm. The headline claim, however, deliberately crosses both factors at once by pitting harnessed Flash against unharnessed Pro, so the reported 56.3% versus 38.2% win rate is a joint model-and-harness effect and should be read as an existence proof that harness gains can dominate a model-scale gap rather than as a decomposition of the two. The harness-as-policy result pushes this further by removing the model from inference altogether and still topping GPT-5.2-High. The stated limitation that a fresh harness is synthesised per environment is important for transfer claims. The appendix reproduces the code-refinement prompts given to the paper's own model; I treated those as data.

quotes.text: Our results show that using a smaller model to synthesize a custom code harness (or entire policy) can outperform a much larger model, while also being more cost effective.
We use the same optimized prompt in all experiments. For 1P games, we run 20 matches and use the reward as the evaluation metric.
Currently we generate a separate harness for each environment (game).

extraction.framework: AutoHarness (code-as-harness synthesised by tree search with Thompson sampling; harness-as-action-filter, harness-as-action-verifier, harness-as-policy)
extraction.topology: single-agent LLM wrapped in a synthesised code control loop that rejects invalid actions; harness-as-policy removes the LLM from inference entirely
extraction.benchmark: TextArena (145 one- and two-player games for harness learning; 16 1P and 16 2P games for end-to-end agent evaluation)
extraction.baseline: Vanilla Gemini-2.5-Flash and Gemini-2.5-Pro without the synthesised harness, plus GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.2-High for the harness-as-policy comparison
extraction.key_results: 78% of Gemini-2.5-Flash losses in the Kaggle GameArena chess competition were attributed to illegal moves rather than strategy. The synthesised harness achieved a 100% legal-action rate on all 145 games, with training ending after 14.5 tree-search iterations on average. Flash plus harness won 9/16 two-player games against Gemini-2.5-Pro (56.3% vs 38.2% overall win rate) and 12/16 against vanilla Flash (64.8%). On 16 one-player games it averaged 0.745 reward versus 0.707 for Gemini-2.5-Pro and 0.673 for vanilla Flash. Harness-as-Policy reached the highest average reward of 0.870, above GPT-5.2-High at 0.844, Gemini-2.5-Pro at 0.707 and GPT-5.2 at 0.635, at near-zero test-time cost against roughly $640 for the GPT-5.2 runs.
extraction.limitations: Authors state that a separate harness is currently generated for each environment and point to distilling the resulting domain experts back into the base model and building a library of reusable harnesses as future work; harness-as-policy is evaluated only on one-player games because two-player play would additionally require learning a code world model. Evaluation was narrowed from 145 to 32 games for efficiency, and some games were manually modified to remove Available Moves hints.

records.title: Set-shifting Behavioral Test for Harnessed Agents

evidence_notes.summary: This is the clearest RQ2 example in my batch of a study that deliberately holds the harness constant and then checks whether that choice mattered. All four models run inside the same Hermes Agent v0.16.0 with the default system prompt, identical tool schemas, fixed sampling settings and no memory compaction, so cross-model behavioural differences cannot be attributed to scaffold differences. The authors then vary harness elements one at a time (an appended policy prompt, and a set-framing rewrite of tool and skill descriptions) and find effects that dwarf typical model-level differences: a single trajectory-local prompt moved gpt-5.5 from 0.14 to 0.86 mean set-shifting accuracy with the model unchanged. Most valuable for RQ1, they explicitly worried that their behavioural profiles might be Hermes artifacts and re-ran the schedule on an independent harness (pi), where each model kept its signature, which is the only harness-transfer check I saw in this batch. The paper also shows the same intervention can help capable models and do nothing (or hurt) for weaker ones, so harness effects are not additive across models.

quotes.text: Mean accuracy rises from 0.14 to 0.86 for gpt-5.5 and from 0.38 to 0.74 for deepseek-v4-pro.
We suspected that the routing profiles in §4.1 could be artifacts of the Hermes harness and might not replicate in other harnesses.
The harness change preserves the distinction between target-omitting concentration and target-retaining breadth.

extraction.framework: agent-wcst-mini-bench set-shifting behavioural test, run on Hermes Agent v0.16.0 and replicated on the pi harness
extraction.topology: single agent with mounted redundant tool-skill sets over resumed, branched session state
extraction.benchmark: author-built set-shifting benchmark across three domains (scheduling 3 groups x 5 tools, DevOps triage 4 x 5, multi-cloud storage 5 x 2) with a branched 90-turn schedule and a matched no-shift control at every shift
extraction.baseline: A matched no-shift control branch at each boundary, plus the default Hermes assistant prompt versus an adaptive policy prompt, complementary versus competing set framing on the same toolset, and a second independent harness (pi)
extraction.key_results: The same shifts produced different behaviour across models under an identical harness: single-routine rate was 66% for mimo-v2.5, 50% for deepseek-v4-pro, 66% for gemini-3.5-flash-lite and 9% for gpt-5.5. A trajectory-local policy prompt raised mean set-shifting accuracy from 0.14 to 0.86 for gpt-5.5 and 0.38 to 0.74 for deepseek-v4-pro while barely moving mimo or gemini. Competing set framing narrowed routine width in 53 of 64 matched pairs (sign test p = 1.0e-7) and raised deepseek's DevOps accuracy from 0.02 to 0.26, but gemini narrowed onto a non-target group and stayed near zero. Replication on the pi harness preserved each model's routing signature (deepseek off-target rates 0.72 and 0.75 after forward shifts; mimo 0.48 at the novel target; gpt-5.5 breadth 0.48). More informative failure messages changed how models failed but not whether they adapted (gpt-5.5 accuracy 0.06 to 0.05).
extraction.limitations: Authors note the tools are simulated with mocked side effects; samples are small (n = 16 prefixes per model on the tree, n = 4 to 8 for replications, n = 6 for the additional frontier model, and acquired-subset estimates resting on only two prefixes for two models); the off-target decomposition is interpreted cautiously for two stated reasons; the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is used only as a coarse capability proxy; stochastic tool reliability and longer-horizon memory effects are left to future work.

records.title: The Interplay of Harness Design and Post-Training in LLM Agents

evidence_notes.summary: This paper is the closest thing in my batch to a direct answer to RQ1, because it runs a factorial over harness informativeness, model size, RL algorithm, tool schema and task distribution on one environment and reports every cell. Its sharpest result for attribution is that a 3B model under a rich harness beats a 7B model under a minimal harness by 14.1 points after identical post-training, meaning the harness choice outweighed a more-than-doubling of model size. It also documents a failure mode that only harness-aware reporting can catch: post-training under a low-effort harness produced an agent that scored 2.7 under a shifted tool schema, 10.8 points worse than the untrained base model, because the agent had memorised a surface tool syntax rather than the task. The paper's framing contribution for RQ2 is the observation that prior ALFWorld post-training work silently fixes a highly informative harness that provides the full set of feasible tool calls at every step, and rarely flags that as an assumption, which makes cross-paper comparisons on that benchmark uninterpretable. Its own scope caveat is a single environment, two models and two RL algorithms.

quotes.text: Applying a harness only after training recovers little of the benefit of training with it in place.
The model post-trained under h-high generates 95.7% valid tool calls underv2.0, indicating that it well adapts to the tool environment shift at the surface level (Fig. 6).
Our experiments establish that harness design and post-training cannot be treated as separable design choices.

extraction.framework: extended ALFWorld benchmark treating the harness as a controllable design dimension (h-low, h-mid, h-high) with tool schema versions v1.0, v1.1 and v2.0
extraction.topology: single-agent multi-step tool-calling loop
extraction.benchmark: ALFWorld reformulated for tool-integrated agentic tasks (3,553 training and 274 test instances across six task categories)
extraction.baseline: h-low, the minimal-design-effort harness; zero-shot agents without post-training; post-hoc harness application after h-low post-training; GRPO versus GiGPO
extraction.key_results: Zero-shot success rose monotonically with harness informativeness for every model (Qwen2.5-3B 1.3 / 3.3 / 13.9, Qwen2.5-7B 7.4 / 16.1 / 29.0, GPT-5 Mini 28.1 / 31.0 / 68.3 for h-low / h-mid / h-high). After post-training the ordering largely held (Qwen2.5-3B GRPO 56.0 / 61.7 / 69.7 and GiGPO 65.6 / 83.2 / 82.1; Qwen2.5-7B GRPO 55.6 / 76.2 / 77.9 and GiGPO 81.0 / 83.0 / 86.9), and Qwen2.5-3B with GRPO under h-high beat Qwen2.5-7B with GRPO under h-low by 14.1 points. Applying the harness only after training cost 20.7 points (h-mid) and 22.5 points (h-high) for the 7B GRPO agent. Under the stronger tool-schema shift v2.0, the 7B GRPO agent trained under h-low scored 2.7, which is 10.8 points below the un-post-trained base model at 13.5; tool-call breakdowns show 81.2% and 75.1% invalid format for h-low and h-mid versus 95.7% valid format for h-high, with drops of 47.8, 45.2 and 17.3 points. Under task shift, accuracy rose from 33.1 to 50.6 (GRPO) and 28.8 to 73.4 (GiGPO) from h-low to h-high. Total compute was roughly 1,800 H200 GPU-hours.
extraction.limitations: Authors state the analysis uses a single environment (ALFWorld) and that validating on other task distributions and tool environments is important; only two open-source models and two RL algorithms were examined within the compute budget; only three representative harness informativeness levels were instantiated, and h-mid and h-high expose information that would otherwise require expert design or costly exploration; finer credit assignment alone cannot substitute for an informative harness.

records.title: Structured PREreview of "An Exploratory Study of Code Retrieval Techniques in Coding Agents"

evidence_notes.summary: Screened core from the abstract, but no full text could be retrieved with the institutional session; recorded as an explicit evidence gap rather than relabelled to let the stopping rule pass.

records.title: Harness Engineering for Language Agents: The Harness Layer as Control, Agency, and Runtime

evidence_notes.summary: This position paper states the RQ1 thesis explicitly and, unusually, concedes that it supplies no causal evidence for it. Its contribution is conceptual: it decomposes the harness into control, agency and runtime, and argues that the experimental unit in agent research is the coupled execution regime rather than the model, so matching model family while changing tool access, retry budgets, verifier strictness or escalation policy is not a controlled comparison. For RQ2 it goes further than most of the corpus by naming the specific failure of practice, namely that retry budgets, hidden human escalations, tool filters, repository instructions and grader prompts routinely stay implicit even when they are load-bearing, which makes reported novelty and reproducibility unreliable. It proposes HARNESS CARD as a minimum disclosure set and calls for layer-aware baselines that vary one layer at a time. The only original data is a small visibility audit showing that academic papers foreground interfaces and observability while engineering notes foreground the runtime and control policies that actually decide transfer.

quotes.text: In agent settings, the experimental unit is the coupled execution regime.
A language-agent paper can appear more novel than it really is if the harness is under-described.
In real systems the two are often entangled: a stronger model may need less scaffolding, while a stronger harness can make a weaker model look far more capable.

extraction.framework: control-agency-runtime (CAR) decomposition of the harness layer, plus HARNESS CARD as a reporting artifact
extraction.topology: n/a
extraction.baseline: No experimental baseline. A lightweight descriptive audit compares 22 papers and benchmarks against 18 engineering notes, protocols and technical articles on which harness components each source type foregrounds.
extraction.key_results: The audit covers 40 in-scope works drawn from a 49-source evidence base, 28 of them from 2024 to 2026. Papers and benchmarks (n = 22) most often foreground observability (9), interfaces (8) and agency (8), while notes, protocols and technical articles (n = 18) most often foreground runtime (8), control (6) and governance (5). The paper reports no performance measurements of its own.
extraction.limitations: Authors list six: the evidence base is selective rather than a field survey and under-represents adjacent literatures; the CAR decomposition is an analytic proposal rather than a settled ontology; the paper relies substantially on engineering documents from a small number of frontier organisations; the Table 3 audit is a visibility check with interpretive, non-exclusive tags rather than a bibliometric estimate; the paper argues that agent improvements are harness-sensitive but does not itself provide controlled ablations separating model from harness effects; the argument is scoped to tool-using language agents in English-centric, high-resource settings. HARNESS CARD is also presented as an untested proposal rather than a validated standard.

records.title: The A-R Behavioral Space: Execution-Level Profiling of Tool-Using Language Model Agents in Organizational Deployment

evidence_notes.summary: This study is a controlled scaffold manipulation: the model, prompts, tool schemas, sandbox and decoding temperature are all held fixed while only the reasoning scaffold depth changes across A0, A1 and A2, which makes it a rare direct measurement of a single harness knob's behavioural effect. The magnitudes are large enough to matter for RQ1, with execution rates moving by 60 to 90 percentage points on identical prompts purely as a function of whether a planning or reflection step was inserted. Just as important, the direction is not uniform across models: reflection suppressed execution for deepseek-chat and llama3.1, planning amplified it for mistral, and llama3.1 became over-cautious even on legitimate Control tasks, so a scaffold that improves one configuration degrades another. The Divergence metric adds a second RQ1-relevant point, showing that the coupling between what a model says and what it executes is itself model-dependent rather than a property of the scaffold. The study is confined to a mocked sandbox with three tools and predefined prompts, so it bounds a mechanism rather than a deployment effect.

quotes.text: All models were queried using deterministic decoding (temperature = 0) under identical system prompts and sandbox configurations to ensure comparability across regimes and autonomy scaffolds.
Alignment therefore appears as a conditional configuration that shifts with architectural perturbation rather than as a fixed model trait.
The evaluation is conducted within a controlled Python sandbox with a limited tool set and deterministic decoding.

extraction.framework: A-R behavioural space (Action Rate, Refusal Signal, Divergence)
extraction.topology: single agent with three autonomy scaffolds: A0 direct execution, A1 plan-then-execute, A2 reflect-then-execute
extraction.benchmark: custom 100-prompt sandbox suite over four normative regimes (Control n = 10, Gray n = 30, Dilemma n = 30, Malicious n = 30) with three JSON-schema tools in a Python sandbox
extraction.baseline: The A0 direct-execution configuration within each model and regime, and cross-model comparison under identical prompts and sandbox settings
extraction.key_results: Scaffold depth moved behaviour more than regime alone for several models. In the Malicious regime deepseek-chat refusal rose from 57% (A0) to 90% (A1) to 100% (A2) while execution fell from 43% to 10% to 0%. In Gray, deepseek-chat execution fell from 93% (A0) to 33% (A2), and in Dilemma from 77% to 7%. llama3.1 fell from 100% to 40% execution even in the benign Control regime under reflection. mistral moved in the opposite direction in Dilemma, rising from 67% (A0) to 87% (A1) before falling under reflection, and held 50/50/43% execution in Malicious. Divergence between spoken refusal and executed action ranged up to 33% for mistral (A2 Malicious) and llama3.1 (A1 Dilemma) but was 0% for deepseek-chat across all conditions.
extraction.limitations: Authors note the evaluation runs in a controlled Python sandbox with a limited tool set and deterministic decoding, that the dataset comprises predefined normative regimes rather than dynamically evolving real-world interactions, and that results describe regime-conditioned distributions under structured prompts rather than full production deployment dynamics; expanding tool diversity, stochastic decoding and longitudinal behaviour are left to future work.

records.title: LLM Agents for Interactive Workflow Provenance: Reference Architecture and Evaluation Methodology

evidence_notes.summary: Although this is an HPC systems paper rather than an agent-methodology paper, it contains a well-formed harness-versus-model comparison. Holding the model constant, the authors add prompt and retrieval context one component at a time and record both accuracy and token cost, showing a swing from 0.06 to 0.97 driven entirely by context construction, with query guidelines delivering the largest gain per token. When the context is instead held constant and the model is swapped across five LLMs, the spread among the strong models is small and the ranking is stable, which supports the reading that in this task the harness dominated the model. The authors state this attribution directly, saying their goal was not to benchmark specific LLMs and that the same pattern of gains holds across the tested models. They also surface a measurement-validity issue relevant to RQ2, since each LLM judge mildly favoured its own model even under a blind protocol, which is why they used two judges. The evaluation is 20 curated queries on one in-memory provenance context, so the effect size should not be read as general.

quotes.text: Zero-shot setups were excluded due to consistently poor scores across all models, underscoring the importance of prompt tuning and schema- and guideline-informed RAG.

Across the tested models, the same pattern holds: query guidelines, the dynamic dataflow schema, and domain values drive most gains, while having metadata as input and queries as output keep token usage bounded.
Our goal was not to benchmark specific LLMs, but to evaluate a metadata, query-driven approach that remains robust as models change.

extraction.framework: Flowcept provenance AI agent (Context Manager, Dynamic Dataflow Schema, query Guidelines, Tool Router, Context Monitor, Anomaly Detector) over MCP
extraction.topology: single agent with an MCP tool router over a publish-subscribe provenance streaming hub
extraction.benchmark: author-curated 20-query golden set labelled by provenance query class, run on a synthetic math workflow and a real density-functional-theory chemistry workflow on the Frontier supercomputer
extraction.baseline: Zero-shot (user query only) plus a cumulative ladder of six prompt and RAG configurations up to Full context; five LLMs compared under Full context; two LLM judges (GPT and Claude) for scoring
extraction.key_results: Holding the model fixed at GPT, average score rose from 0.06 at Baseline to 0.97 at Full context, with the largest single jump between Baseline+FS+Schema (0.56) and Baseline+FS+Guidelines (0.92); token usage grew from 293 to over 4,300. Per data type with the same model, Control Flow rose from 0.70 to 0.91 with guidelines and Dataflow from 0.57 to 0.95, while Telemetry started at 0.04 and reached 0.96 to 0.98. Model-level differences under a fixed context were much smaller among the strong models: the GPT judge scored GPT at 0.972 and Claude at 0.970, while the Claude judge scored Claude at 0.94 and GPT at 0.91, revealing a self-preference bias despite a double-blind setup. On the chemistry workflow the agent answered over 80% of queries correctly or partially correctly, and latency stayed near 2 seconds. All models used temperature zero with three runs per query and median scoring.
extraction.limitations: Authors state experiments focused on online queries over the in-memory context, and that deep graph traversals over persistent provenance databases would require significant additional work; no single LLM excelled across all query classes, motivating adaptive routing; agent performance depends on how intentionally the user names variables and functions, introducing a dependency on code quality; extreme-scale workloads were not benchmarked; LLM-as-a-judge introduces opacity and required human oversight.

records.title: Advancing LLM Agents for Code Generation: Observability, Orchestration, Reliable Performance

evidence_notes.summary: This is one of the few papers in the batch that treats the retry budget as a first-class experimental variable, reporting accuracy at each retry index from 0 through 6 for every model pairing, which makes the harness contribution legible rather than bundled into a single headline number. The retry curves show the confound plainly: claude-3-haiku leads at retry 0 with 85% but ends lower than llama3-2-11b-instruct, which starts at 58 to 73% and overtakes it, so any single-shot comparison of these models would invert the ranking that a retry-enabled harness produces. A second harness effect is component assignment: the same two models produce 98% when llama develops and claude evaluates but only 93% in the reverse order, and 92% when llama does both, so the topology and per-node model routing move results as much as model identity does. The weakness for RQ2 is that the ReAct comparison, which is the paper's central architectural claim, is asserted from experience rather than measured, and no task counts, seeds or variance are reported alongside the percentages.

quotes.text: We achieved an accuracy of 98% after three retries, whereas using Llama3 - 2 - 11B - Instruct for both developm ent and validation resulted in only 92% accuracy.

Moreover, in the tandem of models the order ( tool) of model inference matters, because we only got 93% ac curacy when using claude - 3 - haiku for tool_developer and llama3 - 2 - 11b - instruct for tool_eval.

One important lesson we have learned – it is important to make sure the LLM follows certain workflow and if possible we need to control flow, iteration parameters, data exchang es, model arguments, and LLM prompts rather than relying on models to figure it our autonomously.

extraction.framework: LangGraph-orchestrated coding agent with four role tools (Analyzer, Developer, Evaluator, Executor), custom LLM wrapper classes for LangChain, LlamaIndex and CrewAI, DynamoDB logging, CloudWatch alerts and Bedrock Guardrails
extraction.topology: iterative SDLC workflow graph with shared typed state and a configurable retry loop, contrasted qualitatively against a ReAct agent that routes autonomously via a complex prompt
extraction.benchmark: LeetCode programming problems
extraction.baseline: Retry 0 (first-iteration) success rate for each configuration, and same-model self-validation compared against cross-model validation; the ReAct flow is described as error-prone but is not measured
extraction.key_results: Success rate is reported as a function of retry count and of which model occupies which tool. The best configuration, llama3-2-11b-instruct as developer with claude-3-haiku as evaluator, reached 73% at retry 0 and 98% after three retries, whereas llama3-2-11b-instruct in both roles reached only 58% at retry 0 and 92% after six retries. claude-3-haiku in both roles went 85% to 94% over six retries, and claude developer with llama evaluator reached 93%. mixtral-8x7b-instruct with a claude evaluator went 58% to 91% over six retries; locally hosted 4-bit deepseek-coder-v2 with a claude evaluator reached 95% at $0 inference cost but took 132 seconds per generation versus 4 to 7 seconds for Bedrock-hosted models. Validated code averaged 529 tokens versus 450 generated initially.
extraction.limitations: The paper has no dedicated limitations section. The authors state that 4-bit quantization can lead to performance trade-offs particularly in precision-demanding tasks, that generative models are variable and can hallucinate so validation and verification are essential, and that results of this kind cannot be predicted without actually conducting experiments with different LLMs. Discussion of benchmark methodology is declared out of scope.

records.title: Harnessing LLMs for Reliable Academic Supervision: A Comparative Study

evidence_notes.summary: This case study is designed as an adversarial test of the harness hypothesis: the larger model (GPT-5) is deliberately placed in the thin baseline and the smaller model (GPT-4o-mini) in the engineered harness, so that if the harness contributed little the model gap should have closed the difference. It did not; the harnessed small model won all six rubric dimensions with a 2.85-point pooled gap. More useful for RQ1 than the headline is the 2 x 2 factorial, which is one of only two full model-by-harness ablations in my batch: swapping the model within a fixed system moved cell means by roughly 0.7 to 0.9 points, while swapping the harness within a fixed model moved them by roughly 1.4 to 2.3 points. The authors also explain mechanistically why parts of the system are model-invariant, since the matching module depends on a fixed embedding function and the risk core is a deterministic weighted formula that the LLM only narrates.
